pages.body:
# Guide

The Guide explains the interface and functionality across the produuz.it platform. Use these pages as a reference for each feature area.

## Sections

- **[Viewer](/guide/viewer/)** — The 3D production viewer: visualize designs, track checklists, and manage station workflows.
- **[Properties in Texts](/guide/properties/)** — The `{property}` names you can use in the viewer header, the list hint and the machine file fields.
- **[Management](/guide/management/)** — Company settings, users, projects, production lines, IFC parsing setup, and machines.
- **[Dashboard](/guide/management/dashboard/)** — Production indicators for managers.
- **[Reports](/guide/reports/)** — Generate Bills of Materials, production spreadsheets, quality control reports, QR stickers, and more.
- **[Machine Files](/guide/machine_files/formats/panel_mob1/)** — File formats and machine configurations for CNC equipment (MOB, BTL, XCS, DXF, etc.).
- **[Production Planning](/guide/planning/)** — Schedule constructibles on a calendar with drag-and-drop and workload tracking.
- **[Quantities](/guide/quantities/)** — Plan design quantities across project phases and batches.
- **[Issues Management](/guide/issues/)** — Track production issues and quality control records.
- **[Logistics](/guide/logistics/)** — Material tracking, part batches and kits.
- **[Delivery & Racks](/guide/logistics/delivery/)** — Rack setups, rack loads and the Delivery screen.
- **[Sizes and Materials](/guide/stock/)** — Manage your material catalog: materials, sizes, and products.
- **[Integrations & Webhooks](/guide/integrations/)** — Receive notifications in external systems when events occur.
- **[Account Settings](/guide/account/)** — Personal settings, 2FA, and notification preferences.
- **[API](/guide/api/)** — REST API overview, authentication, and available endpoints.
- **[Claude connector (MCP)](/guide/mcp/)** — Ask Claude about your production data.

pages.title: Viewer
pages.body:
# 3D Viewer

The Viewer is the main production interface in produuz.it. It displays 3D models and technical drawings of your constructibles (assemblies and modules), and provides tools for managing production checklists, issues, logistics, and more.

[[toc]]

## Accessing the Viewer

Pick **Prod** in the mode toggle at the top of the left menu, then tap a constructible in the list. The mode toggle shows only the modes your account can use (**Manage**, **Logistics**, **Prod** and **Delivery**).

The Viewer has two modes, chosen in the list filter described below:

- **Production** — For constructibles in production. Includes checklists, issues, QR, RFID and rack features.
- **Design** — For reviewing designs before production. Shows 3D models and drawings in read-only mode, without production tools. Production users do not have this mode.

::: info
If your company has **Forced time registration in viewer** switched on, production users see a *Constructible not started* message instead of the 3D model and the drawings until they start the panel from the checklist.
:::

## The list on the left

The left menu holds the queue: every constructible you can work on, in the order production follows. What sits above that list depends on how you are working.

### Working by date

With no project selected, and if your company works by date, the header shows the **date selector**: arrows for the previous and next day, and a dropdown with a calendar and two switches: **Show delayed constructibles**, to include constructibles that are late, and **Max number of constructibles**, to cap how many are listed at a time (between 5 and 50).

### Working by project

With a project selected, the header shows one control for everything that decides what the list holds. Closed, it tells you where you are:

- the phase on the top line and the batch on the bottom one, or *All phases* / *All batches* when nothing is filtered;
- how many constructibles of what is listed are ready, out of the total;
- a `×` to clear the filter in one tap, when a filter is set.

The arrows step to the previous and next batch, continuing into the next phase when you reach the end of one.

Tapping the button opens it:

- **Production / Design** at the top, for managers and admins. Production lists the panels and modules being built; Design lists the designs, read-only. In Design mode there are no batches, so the phase and batch list is not shown.
- **All** clears the filter.
- Tap a **phase** to see its batches only.
- Tap a **batch** to work on that batch alone.
- Every row shows how many of its constructibles are ready. The count turns green once they all are, so a finished batch or phase is easy to spot. Batches with nothing in them are greyed out, marked *Empty*, and never count as finished.
- The **Show ready constructibles** switch at the bottom shows or hides constructibles that are already finished. The menu stays open while you use it, so you can compare.

![The list filter, opened](./viewer-list-selector.svg)

1. **Production** or **Design**, for managers and admins.
2. A finished phase: its count is green.
3. The batch you are working on.
4. A batch with nothing in it.
5. Show or hide the constructibles that are already finished.

The constructible you currently have open always stays in the list, even when the filter would leave it out, so you never lose your place.

### Rows of the list

Each row shows the design name and revision, the position of the constructible in its batch (for example **3**/12), the first characters of its id and a *phase | batch* chip. Below that:

- a green **Ready** chip once the constructible is finished;
- otherwise one numbered chip per station of your production line: outlined while the station has not started, orange while it is working, green when it is ready, grey when the constructible does not pass through it;
- a kit chip (for example *13 parts left* or *Kitted parts*) when your company tracks kits;
- the delivery state once the constructible has been loaded on a rack.

A red chip with a date marks a constructible that is late. Multipanel groups have a row of their own, placed just before their first panel.

## Layout

![The production viewer in the Extended view](./viewer-layout.svg)

1. The account button. It shows who is working. See [Who is working](#who-is-working).
2. The mode toggle.
3. The list filter. See [Working by project](#working-by-project).
4. The open constructible, with one chip per station.
5. The zones and the 3D tools. See [3D Model](#_3d-model).
6. Front and back view.
7. **3D** and the drawings of the constructible. See [Technical Drawings](#technical-drawings).
8. Switch between the Extended and the Standard view.
9. The toolbar.
10. The checklist of your station. See [Checklist](#checklist).
11. The part lists and the data of the part you picked.

The Viewer uses a three-panel layout:

| Panel | Content |
|-------|---------|
| **Left** | 3D model or technical drawing (PDF) |
| **Center** | Vertical toolbar with action buttons |
| **Right** | Extended view only: the checklist on top, then the part lists and part data when the left panel shows the 3D model, or detail drawings and documents when it shows a drawing |

There are two views, switched with the **Extended** / **Standard** button at the top of the toolbar:

- **Extended** — All three panels. The right panel shows the panel checklist at the top and the usual drawing underneath, so a worker can tick tasks off with the drawing in front of them. The checklist button is not in the toolbar in this view: it would only open the same tasks in a dialog.
- **Standard** — Left panel + toolbar. The drawing takes all the width, and the checklist goes back to being a button in the toolbar. Detail drawings and documents open full screen from buttons at the bottom of the toolbar.

Extended is the default on big screens, standard on phones and small tablets, and your choice is remembered on that device. Both views are available on any screen. On a phone the toolbar becomes a bar at the bottom of the screen: tap the arrow to open it and see all the buttons.

## 3D Model

![The 3D model and its controls](./viewer-3d.svg)

1. The zones: tap one to show or hide it.
2. Measurement.
3. Clipping plane.
4. Recenter.
5. Look at the panel from the front or from the back.

### Controls

- **Rotate** — Click and drag to rotate the model.
- **Zoom** — Use the scroll wheel.
- **Pan** — Right-click and drag to move around.
- **Recenter** — Click the recenter button at the top right to reset the view.
- **Front / Back** — Buttons under the top-right controls to look at the panel from the front or from the back.

### Selecting Parts

Click any part in the 3D model to select it. In the Extended view the right panel shows its data, including:

- Zone, reference and material, as chips at the top
- Dimensions (width, height, length, thickness), finish and comment
- Branch, category and the custom part classes that recognised it
- IFC properties and property sets
- Creation date and revision number

Click **Part data** to fold or unfold the details. If the part has part drawings, they are shown under **Drawing**: tap one to open it full screen, or tap **3d** to turn the part around in 3D.

### Zone Selection

Use the zone toggle buttons at the top right to show or hide specific zones of the constructible. This is useful for focusing on a specific area during production. When a constructible opens, the zones assigned to your station are selected; if your station has none, all zones are.

For modules, you can also filter by sub-assembly using the assembly dropdown.

### Advanced Tools

- **Measurement** — Click the ruler button, then double-click on the model to place the points of a measurement. Click the ruler again to go back to selecting parts.
- **Clipping Plane** — Click the clipping button (next to the ruler), then double-click a face of the model to place a cutting plane that reveals the interior structure. Click the button again to remove the plane.

![A clipping plane across the panel](./viewer-clipping.svg)

1. The clipping button turns orange while the plane is on.
2. The plane, placed on the face you double-clicked. The arrow shows the side that is cut away.

## Technical Drawings

![A drawing open in the left panel](./viewer-drawing.svg)

1. The pages of a drawing with several.
2. The drawing buttons. The lighter one was generated by produuz.it.
3. Recenter.

The left panel can switch between the 3D model and technical drawings (PDFs). Use the buttons at the bottom of the left panel: **3D** for the model, and one button per drawing.

- When your station has drawings assigned, only those are listed, and the station's default drawing opens on its own.
- Drawings generated automatically by produuz.it have a lighter button than uploaded ones.
- Multi-page drawings show arrows and a page counter to move between pages.
- The recenter button at the top right resets the zoom.

## Bill of Materials (BOM)


When the left panel shows the 3D model, the right panel starts with **Part lists** for the current assembly: one button per branch (**Timber**, **Plate** and your custom branches). While the model is still being analysed, a message says to wait a few minutes.

### Part List

Tap a branch to open its **Bill of Materials** table. Parts with the same reference, material, comment and finish share one row, with these columns: **REF** (with the part category chips), **Material**, **Count**, **Size**, **Length**, **Comment**, **Finish** and **Zone**. **Select** highlights those parts in the 3D model.

![The Bill of Materials of the timber branch](./viewer-bom.svg)

1. The reference and the category of the part.
2. **Select** highlights these parts in the 3D model.

### Unknown Parts

Next to the branch buttons, lighter buttons list the parts found in the model file but not in the database, per branch, plus an **unknown** button for the rest. This helps identify parts that may need to be added to the system.

### Part Drawings

When a part is selected, its part drawings are shown under the part data. See [Selecting Parts](#selecting-parts).

## Production Features

::: info
Production features are only available in **Production** mode (not in Design mode).
:::

### Checklist

![The checklist of one station](./viewer-checklist.svg)

1. Who is working. See [Who is working](#who-is-working).
2. The station tabs. A green check marks a finished station.
3. A ticked task, with who ticked it and when.
4. A task that needs a picture: the photos taken so far, the camera button and the browse button.
5. A task with a form. The red dot means the form is still empty.
6. A task that needs a QR code.
7. **Station job completed**, enabled once every task is ticked.

The checklist shows the production progress for the current constructible at the selected station. In the Standard view it opens from the **Tasks** button in the toolbar; in the Extended view it sits at the top of the right panel.

- **Tasks button** — Says *Not started*, *Paused*, *Ready*, or how many tasks are done (for example `3 of 8`). The bar under it is red when the panel is not started, orange while it is in progress, and fills green as tasks are ticked. Under the button, a scrolling line shows your station and the next task.
- **Header** — The station tabs (a green check marks a finished station) and the names of who is working. See [Who is working](#who-is-working).
- **Task list** — Each task has a checkbox, and may require:
  - QR code scanning
  - A picture (see below)
  - Filling a custom form
  - Reviewing associated documents

**Tasks that need a picture**

The task row has a **camera button** and a **browse button**, on every device.

- On an Android tablet or phone, the camera button opens the device's own camera
  app: take the photo, confirm, and you are back on the checklist.
- On a computer or a Windows tablet it opens the camera in a small window — one
  click to open, one to shoot.
- The browse button picks a photo you already have. On a computer you can also
  drag files onto the row or paste a screenshot into it.

::: tip The camera button opens the gallery instead?
Some companies manage their tablets with a policy that blocks the camera app.
The app cannot tell that apart from a working camera, so it asks and the device
answers with the photo gallery. An admin can switch on **Avoid native camera in
viewer** under the **Settings** button of the company page, and the app will take
the picture itself instead of asking the device.
:::

- The photo is stored **exactly as the camera took it**, at full resolution. It
  is the quality record of the panel, so nothing is shrunk or re-compressed.
- **The task ticks itself** when the photo is stored, as long as nothing else is
  missing — a form still to fill or a QR still to scan keeps it unticked. You can
  always untick it.
- The photos stay visible **after** the task is ticked, as thumbnails. Tap one to
  see the picture full size. **Clean** removes them. A photo taken before this
  feature existed gets its thumbnail the first time somebody opens the panel, so
  an old panel with many pictures fills in over a couple of visits.
- Each thumbnail says **who uploaded it** when you hover or press it. See:
  [Quality Control Report](/guide/reports/quality_control/)
- If the upload fails you get a message, the thumbnail disappears and the task is
  **not** ticked, so a missing photo can never look like a stored one.

**Actions:**

Tasks can only be ticked once the panel and the station are started. Depending on the state, the checklist shows one of these:

- **Start production** — The panel has not been started yet. This starts it at your station. If your company tracks kits and parts are missing, a warning (*The kit is not complete*) lets you **Start anyway** or **Cancel**.
- **Force start station** — Shown instead when you are at a later station and the previous stations are not finished. After you confirm, the previous stations are marked as ready and yours is started.
- **Start station** — The panel is under way, but your station has not started it yet.
- **Resume** — The panel is paused.
- **Pause** — Temporarily stop work.
- **Station job completed** — Mark the station as done (enabled when all tasks are checked). At the last station of the line the button reads **Panel ready** and finishes the constructible.

When the station is done, the checklist shows *Job for your station is completed*.

### Multiwall Checklist

When you open a Multipanel Group in the viewer, the toolbar shows a group **Tasks** button instead of the per-panel one. It gathers the checklist of every panel of the group at the currently selected station, so a worker can drive the whole multiwall from a single screen.

- **Progress** — The button shows how many panels of the group are loaded (for example `4 / 5`) and the combined progress for the current station across all of them.
- **Start** — If some panels are not started at this station, a banner says how many and offers **Start all panels**.
- **Tasks** — Each task has a heading with a chip that shows on how many panels it is ticked (`3 / 5`). Under it there is one row per panel, labelled with the panel name, so each panel can be ticked, photographed or filled in on its own.
- **Check all** — Simple tasks (no picture, form or QR field) have a **Check all** button that ticks the task on every panel at once.
- **Station switcher** — The station tabs in the dialog header move the whole group between stations.
- **Station job completed** / **Panel ready** — Enabled once every task is ticked on every panel.

![The checklist of a multipanel group](./viewer-multiwall.svg)

1. How many panels of the group are loaded.
2. Some panels are not started at this station: **Start all panels** starts them.
3. A simple task: one row per panel, and **Check all** ticks it on every panel.
4. A task with a picture is done panel by panel.

### Station Switching

Tap the station tabs at the top of the checklist, or open the account button at the top of the left menu and choose **Change Station** to pick any station of any line. For production users the tabs only allow the previous stations, and the next one once your station is ready. If you open a station whose previous stations are not finished, the checklist offers **Force start station** (see above).

### Issues

![The Note button: a new issue](./viewer-new-issue.svg)

1. The constructible the issue is attached to, and the engineering contact of the project.
2. *Production Issue* or *Quality Control Issue*.
3. Make the issue visible in the viewer for every worker.
4. Also send it to chosen colleagues in the chat.
5. Pictures and files, with the camera and browse buttons.
6. Add the data of the parts selected in the 3D model to the text.

Two buttons in the toolbar deal with issues:

- **Note** — Create a new issue for this constructible. Pick a **Category** (*Production Issue* or *Quality Control Issue*), enter a **Title** and **Content**, and add pictures or files with the camera and browse buttons. **Attach part info** adds the data of the parts selected in the 3D model to the text. **Send message to** sends the issue to chosen colleagues in the chat. Tick **Show in viewer to everybody.** to make the issue visible in the viewer for every worker.
- **Issues** — Lists the production issues of this constructible that were marked *Show in viewer to everybody.* The badge shows how many there are. Tap one to see its text, category, status, user, creation date, whether it is solved, and its pictures.

### QR Code

Click the QR button to display a QR code for the current constructible, and **Print** to print it. It can be attached to the physical item for quick identification on the shop floor.

### RFID Tag

Click the RFID button to register an RFID tag code for the current constructible. You can type the code, or press **Scan QR** to read the QR code printed on the tag with the camera.

### Rack / Logistics

The **Rack** button only appears when the constructible is on a rack load. It turns green and reads **In rack** once the constructible is loaded. It opens the **Rack Arrangement**:

- the rack load, its rack, the position of this constructible and how many panels are loaded;
- a warning when the panel is not finished yet, or when other panels must go on the rack before it;
- a drawing of the rack and the list of panels on the load, in loading order;
- **Mark loaded** and **Mark not loaded** at the bottom.

## Who is working

Several people often share one tablet account. So that the records name the person and not the tablet, each person has an **alias** (for example `JAN`), and the account keeps a list of the people who may work under it (**Production employees**). Both are set in **Company settings → User accounts**.

To say who is at the station right now:

1. Open the account button at the top of the left menu and choose **Change employees**, or tap the names in the checklist header.
2. The **Select employees** dialog shows one card per person, with the alias, the name and your company's own id for that person. The card of the account itself has a key icon and says *this account*.
3. Tap every person who is working. Tap again to deselect. **Clean** deselects everybody.
4. Press **Save**.

![The Select employees dialog](./viewer-employees.svg)

1. The account itself: pick it when the work should be filed under the account.
2. A selected person.

**Change employees** only appears when more than one person can work under the account. With a single person there is nothing to choose, and that person is used automatically. If nobody is selected, the work is recorded under the account itself.

Once saved, the aliases are shown:

- on the account button, in orange, instead of the username (`JAN · PIET`, or `JAN +2` for more than two people);
- in the checklist header, as chips (in the Extended view, one chip with the number of people);
- on every ticked task, with the time: `JAN · PIET · 10:02`;
- on each picture, as *Uploaded by*.

The same names appear in the [Quality Control Report](/guide/reports/quality_control/) and in the Production Proof card of the constructible.

## Specifications & Documents

- **Spec** — When the constructible has a specification, a **Spec** button appears in the toolbar (or a list of buttons, one per specification). Press and hold it to see the document; release to close it.
- **DETS / DOCS** — The button at the bottom of the toolbar switches the files offered for this constructible between detail drawings (**DETS**) and documents (**DOCS**). In documents mode the Bill of Materials files generated for it are listed too. In the Extended view the files open in the right panel; in the Standard view they open full screen.

pages.title: Properties in Texts
pages.body: # Properties in texts Several text fields in Produuz.it are **templates**: you type free text, and wherever you want a value from the model you write a property name between curly braces. ``` Project: {project_name} - Phase: {phase_name} ``` becomes ``` Project: Zonnehof - Phase: Fase 2 ``` Every field that works this way has an **Insert property** button ({ }) on its right. It lists everything you can use in that field, including your own model properties, and inserts it where the cursor is. That button is the authoritative list — this page is the same list, written down. ![The Insert property menu](./insert-property.svg) 1. The **Insert property** button at the end of the field. 2. Your own model properties, read from your panels. [[toc]] ## Where you can use them | Where | Field | Resolved per | |-------|-------|--------------| | Company → Viewer settings | **Custom Viewer Header** | Panel | | Company → Viewer settings | **Custom List Hint** (the second line in the viewer list) | Panel | | Company → Viewer settings | **Custom Constructibles Table Column** | Panel | | Machine setup → BTL / BTLx / BVX | **Part data fields** (Designation, Assembly number, Group, Package, Material, Timber grade, Quality grade, Subgroup / Storey) | Part | | Machine setup → BTL / BTLx / BVX | **User attribute values** (up to 5) | Part | The two groups use **two different lists**, because they are resolved against two different things. A viewer header describes a panel; a BTL Designation describes one piece of timber inside that panel. Read the right table below. ## Panel properties Used by the viewer header, the list hint and the custom constructibles column. | Property | Value | |----------|-------| | `{design_name}` | Design name of the panel | | `{priority}` | Priority inside the batch | | `{batch_name}` | Batch name | | `{phase_name}` | Phase name | | `{scheduled_prod_date}` | Scheduled production date | | `{client_order_id}` | Client order id | | `{project_name}` | Project name | | `{project_number}` | Project number | | `{super_project}` | Super project | | `{client_name}` | Client name | Plus **your own properties** — see below. ## Part properties Used by the machine file fields (BTL, BTLx and BVX). These are resolved **per part**, so a single file covering a whole batch still carries the right panel name on every piece. | Property | Value | |----------|-------| | `{part_pos}` | Part reference / position | | `{name}` | Part name | | `{material}` | Material | | `{description}` | Part description | | `{erp_mat}` | ERP material code | | `{comment}` | Comment | | `{finish}` | Finish | | `{width}` / `{height}` / `{length}` | Dimensions | | `{unit}` | Unit | | `{profile_size}` | Profile size | | `{shaped_section_name}` | Shaped section name | | `{zone}` | Zone | | `{assembly_name}` | Panel name | | `{design_name}` | Panel name — the same value as `{assembly_name}` | | `{batch}` | Batch name | | `{phase}` | Phase name | | `{project_name}` | Project name | | `{project_number}` | Project number | | `{super_project_name}` | Super project | | `{client_order_id}` | Client order id | Plus **your own properties** — see below. ::: tip The panel names also work here `{super_project}`, `{batch_name}` and `{phase_name}` — the names the panel list above uses — are accepted in machine file fields too, and give the same value as `{super_project_name}`, `{batch}` and `{phase}`. You do not have to remember which list you are in. ::: ## Your own properties Both lists also accept **any property of your own models**. These are the keys stored on a panel as metadata or client metadata: whatever your IFC parsing setup extracts, or whatever your ERP writes through the API. They are different at every company — `{montagevolgorde}` is a real property at one company and a typo at every other. Two ways to see yours: - The **Insert property** button lists them under *Your own properties*. It is read from your own panels, so if the section is empty it means none of your panels carry properties of their own — not that the list failed to load. - On any panel: **Constructibles → open the panel → Client meta**. ## Rules - **A property that does not exist is not an error.** In the viewer settings it renders as `---`; in machine files it renders empty. Nothing fails, so a typo is silent — which is exactly why the Insert property button exists. - **Free text is kept as it is.** `Order {client_order_id} - {design_name}` gives `Order ORD-88 - HD-529`. - **Every property must be named.** `{}` and `{0}` are not accepted, and the field will say so before you can save. - **Every brace must be closed.** `{design_name` is rejected the same way. - **To print a literal brace**, double it: {{ gives `{`. - **Numbers can be padded**: `{priority:03d}` gives `007`. This only works on numeric properties. - **Your own properties cannot override the ones in the tables above.** If one of your model properties is called `design_name`, `{design_name}` still means the design name.

pages.title: Management
pages.body:
# Management - Company Settings

<!-- [[toc]] -->

Open **Company settings** from the **Settings** section of the left menu, in company-wide mode. Company managers and admins can open it. Editing the company info, the interface settings, the backups and the work calendar is reserved for admins.

## Main settings

### Company info

Company info such as name, address and emails is shown on reports, mails and other templates. Company notifications are sent to the "Contact email". Admins change it with **EDIT INFO** on the company card.

### Interface settings

Admins open these with **SETTINGS** on the company card. The dialog has two blocks, *Interface/Viewer Settings* and *Company Workflow Settings*.

![The company Settings dialog](./company-settings.svg)

1. *Interface/Viewer Settings*.
2. A text field that takes `{property}` names, with its **Insert property** button.
3. *Company Workflow Settings*.
4. **Kitted parts**. See [Kitted Parts](/guide/logistics/#kitted-parts).

*Interface/Viewer Settings*

* **Use corporate color in the interface**: the same switch as in the Styles card (see [Styles](#styles)).
* **Show QR button**: Show a button in the panel viewer that gives the user a QR for the panel.
* **Show RFID button**: Show a button in the panel viewer that gives the option to register RFID tags.
* Hiding parts in the 3D viewer is no longer a company setting. It is a **custom part class** in your parsing setup: give the class the rules that recognise those parts and turn on *Hide in the 3D viewer*. That way each setup decides for itself, instead of one switch deciding for the whole company. The old *Hide 'Hidden Materials' in 3D* checkbox is still in the dialog; use the part class instead. See: [Custom part classes](/guide/management/ifcps/#custom-part-classes)
* **Show project number in the project selector**: Adds the project number above the project name in the project selector, and next to the project name in the views that list projects from several projects at once. The number is left out when the project name or the superproject already starts with it. With this on, the selector also gets a search box that matches name, number and superproject.
* **Avoid native camera in viewer**: pictures are taken inside the app instead of opening the device's camera. Turn it on only if your tablets are managed by a policy that blocks the camera app, which makes the camera button open the photo gallery.
* **Language**: the default language for the app. Users can change the language if they are allowed by the admin (see the Users table).
* **Custom Viewer Header**, **Custom List Hint** and **Custom Constructibles Table Column**: replace the panel header in the viewer, the second line of each row in the viewer list, and add a column to the constructibles table, with a text you write using placeholders. See: [Properties in Texts](/guide/properties/)
* **Zones from 10 are subzones**: in the 3D viewer, zones from 10 upwards are shown together with their main zone (zone 10 with zone 1, zone -25 with zone -2, and so on).

*Company Workflow Settings*

* **Production list based on dates**: production works from a list per day instead of per project.
* **Forced time registration in viewer**: production users have to start the checklist of a panel before they can work on it in the viewer.
* **Launch analysis automatically**: on by default. New designs are analysed as soon as their files arrive.
* **Best effort panel orientation**: off by default. When the parsing setup cannot place a panel, its orientation is worked out from the geometry. The front face may come out on the wrong side; machine files never use it.
* **Kitted parts**: *Off* (no kit tracking), *Manual* (the operator marks a constructible kitted from the logistics viewer) or *Automatic*, marked *Recommended* (a constructible is kitted when all its parts are ready).
* **autoreference** (a select): how panel references are set: from the parsing setup, generated automatically, or from the parsing setup with the automatic reference as fallback (the default).

## Licenses

Gives an overview of the licensing: the maximum number of licenses per product, with how many are in use where it applies (for example `3/5`), and which modules the company has.

## Styles

Corporate color and logos can be changed. They are also used in PDF generation. Sticker banner is a wide logo to be used in some of the sticker presets (like panel QR stickers).

Once you pick a corporate color it is used across the interface (buttons, links, scrollbars) and in PDF generation. If you prefer the standard produuz.it orange in the interface, untick "Use corporate color" next to the color picker — the color is kept and still used in PDFs.

## Projects

Projects are managed in **Projects Settings**, in the **Settings** section of the left menu. Projects are fabrication sets; we recommend no more than 100 designs and 500 panels per project for performance reasons. The more panels in a project, the slower the interface gets.

Some large projects do not fit in those numbers, so we introduced the "superproject" parameter, so you can group several projects under the same key name. For example, you may have a big project with 10 buildings, and you may want to split it into 10 projects that belong to the same superproject.

Projects can be "archived" 🗃. Archived projects are hidden from the user and only visible in the archive. To keep a full copy of archived projects, include them in a [company backup](/guide/management/backup/).

Each project can have an **engineering contact** — the person to reach with questions about it, typically the responsible engineer. In the project form (and in Project Settings), pick an existing contact or create a new one on the spot. Once set, it is shown to production staff in the issue detail panel (see [Contacts](#contacts)).

## Users

The **User accounts** table lists everyone in the company: the people who log in and the production employees who do not. Its columns are Alias, Username, Login, Email, Role, Production station, Prod. Employees, Licenses and Actions.

### User form

* **Alias**: required. How this person is identified in the factory; shown on the checklist and in the reports.
* **Username**: used to log in, and unique across produuz.it. Leave it empty for someone who does not log in.
* 🌐 **Multilanguage**: the user can change the language of the interface.
* 👁 **Hide panel queue**: if checked, the user sees only the designs mode in the viewer, not the panel list.
* 🔃 **Can change station**: the user can switch to another station.
* 🔄 **Can change production line**: the user can switch to another production line.
* 🌴 **Has own holidays**: if checked, the user does not get the company holidays. Only the user's own holidays are used.
* 🔨 **Has own worktime**: if checked, the user's own entries have priority over the company entries. This means that if you set a worktime with start and end date, all days outside this range will take company worktime.

::: info Work Calendar
More about holidays and worktime in [Work Calendar](#work-calendar)
:::


## Contacts

Contacts are people to reach about a project, such as the responsible engineer. A contact has a name, phone and email, and is **not** a system user.

Manage them in the **Contacts** table, below User accounts. You can also add a contact directly from the project form when assigning one.

A project can have an **engineering contact** (set in the project form or in Project Settings). When it does, that contact is shown to production staff in the issue detail panel, so they know who to reach with questions about an issue.

## API accounts

The **API Accounts** table, below Contacts, holds the accounts that external systems use to connect to produuz.it. See [API accounts](/guide/api/#api-accounts).

## Machines

Machines represent CNC equipment or automated stations in your production lines. Each machine setup has a model (e.g., Mobi One) and a configuration that defines how machine files are generated.

Machine setups live in **Production Settings > Machine Settings** in the left menu. A setup is linked to a station, or to a whole production line, in **Production Settings > Production lines**.

::: tip
For details on configuring production lines, stations, and machines, see the [Production Lines](/guide/management/production_lines/) reference page.
:::

## Work Calendar

The work calendar controls how production time is calculated across the system. It defines working hours and holidays at both the company and user level.

The **Work calendar** card is at the bottom of Company settings and is visible to admins only.

- **Company holidays**: Default holidays that apply to all users (pick the non working days in the calendar).
- **Company worktime**: Default working hours and breaks (start/end times per weekday), added with **Add entry**.
- **User-level overrides**: Individual users can have their own holidays and worktime entries (configured in the Users form with the "Has own holidays" and "Has own worktime" checkboxes).

pages.title: Dashboard
pages.body:
# Dashboard

The Dashboard is a management area that gathers production indicators in one place. It is visible in company-wide mode and reserved for managers and admins.

::: info Early preview
The Dashboard is in early preview. New charts and indicators will be added over time.
:::

## How to open it

In the left menu, switch to company-wide mode and click **Dashboard** at the top of the list.

## Choosing the charts

The cog button at the top right opens **Dashboard settings**, a list of every chart grouped by theme (Events, Throughput, Pipeline, Quality, Projects, Planning). Untick a chart to hide it, or untick a group to hide all its charts. The choice is remembered on this device.

![The Dashboard](./dashboard.svg)

1. **Dashboard settings**: pick the charts you want to see.
2. The period of the chart.
3. What your factory could start building today.

## Charts

### Today's activity

A timeline of today's events since midnight, with one lane per production line and a **Now** marker. It shows panels and modules marked ready, stations finished, and issues opened or resolved. The counter next to the title gives the number of events, and the refresh button reloads them.

### Assemblies marked ready

A chart that shows how many panels each production line marked as ready, stacked by line.

- The selector at the top right picks the period: **Last 14 days** (one mark per day), **Last 12 weeks** (the default, one mark per ISO week, Monday-based), or a whole year (this year and the two before).
- Lines with no ready events in the period are not shown.

Use this chart to compare throughput between lines, spot drops or peaks, and check whether weekly production is keeping a steady pace.

### Active backlog

Assemblies still to produce, per production line, split by status: *Waiting*, *Working* and *Locked*. Panels already ready are not counted.

### Ready to build

Unbuilt panels per production line, split by whether their material is there: *Kitted parts*, *Partly cut*, *Not cut yet* and *No parts recorded*. The large number at the top says how many can be built now, out of all still to build. This chart only appears when the company tracks kitted parts (see [Company settings](/guide/management/#interface-settings)).

### Pending delivery

Produced assemblies that are not mounted yet, per production line, split by delivery status: *Unknown*, *In rack* and *Delivered*.

### Issues opened vs resolved

Issues opened and issues resolved per week, over the last 12 weeks.

### Station throughput

Checklist items completed per station, one bar per week, over the last 4 weeks.

### Projects

Active projects against archived ones, with the total.

### Projects by client

How the current projects are spread over clients. Clients beyond the eight largest are grouped under *Other*.

### Design types

How many assembly and module designs there are of each type.

### On-time production and Forecast vs progress

These two charts appear only when the company works by dates (*Production list based on dates* in Company settings).

- **On-time production**: per week over the last 12 weeks, the share of panels marked ready on or before their scheduled production date, against a 100% target line. Panels with no scheduled date are left out.
- **Forecast vs progress**: for this week and the three after it, the panels scheduled that week, split into *Done*, *In progress* and *Pending*.

pages.title: Production Lines
pages.body:
# Production Lines

A company must have at least one production line defined in the system.

**Production Settings** is a group in the **Settings** section of the left menu, in company-wide mode, with three views. **Production lines** holds the lines and their stations. **Machine Settings** holds the machine setups. **Automations** holds the webhooks, the action triggers and the setups they run: machine files and drawings.

File generation templates are not here — they live in **File settings**, under the Files section of the menu. See [Reports](/guide/reports/).

## The Production lines view

The view starts with a **New Production Line** tile. Below it, each production line is a row: a header with its name, what it builds, its machine, its client IDs, its counts (stations, checklist items, machines, worktime capacity) and its actions (edit, copy, delete), and below it the cards of its stations in the order the line runs them.

Rows can be collapsed with the arrow on the left. They all start open, and the ones you collapse stay collapsed the next time you open the view.

Lines are grouped by what they build: modules first, then assemblies, then parts. A line that builds more than one of these appears once, under the largest one. Lines with an unrecognised tipo go to a last group, *Other*.

![A production line row](./production-lines-view.svg)

1. The name of the line and what it builds.
2. The machine of the line. In grey italics when it is read from the line's only machine station.
3. The counts: stations, checklist items, machines and worktime capacity.
4. The drag handle and the position of the station in the line.
5. A station that is in several lines.
6. The two tiles to add a station. See [Working with stations](#working-with-stations).

### The production line form

The production line (PL) itself has the following fields:

- **Name**: A name to identify the PL.
- **Client ID**: An optional list of external identifiers used to link the production line to external systems (e.g. ERP or planning software). Multiple IDs can be added when the line needs to be matched from more than one external source.
- **Tipo**: The assembly, module or part categories that the PL can produce. At least one is required.
- **Line machine**: see [The machine of a line](#the-machine-of-a-line).
- **Worktime Capacity**: the capacity of the line, in minutes.
- **Stations**: on the right side of the form, the stations of the line in order. **Add station** adds an existing station, you drag a station to change the order, and its menu removes it from the line.

![The production line form](./line-form.svg)

1. What the line builds. At least one is required.
2. The line machine. See [The machine of a line](#the-machine-of-a-line).
3. The stations of the line, in order. Drag to reorder; the menu removes a station from the line.

Production lines (PLs) are expected to have at least 1 station. Stations represent steps in the production process.

### Working with stations

At the end of every line there are two tiles:

- **New Production station** creates a station and adds it to that line.
- **Add existing station** lists every station that is not already in the line, including the ones with no line at all.

A station card shows its position in the line, its name, its client station ID, its number of checklist items, its expected worktime, its machine (or *Manual* when it has none), when it is enabled, and its zones, branches, assembly prefixes and drawing numbers when it has any.

**Reordering** is done by dragging a station card by its handle. The new order is saved as soon as you drop the card. You cannot drag a card from one line into another: to move a station, add it to the new line and then remove it from the old one.

A station can belong to **several lines** at once. It then gets a card in each of them, marked **Shared**, and its cards list the lines it is in. It is the same station in all of them, so editing it from any line changes it everywhere. Its position, on the other hand, belongs to each line separately.

Stations that belong to **no line** are listed at the end of the view, under *No production line*. This is normal — a station can be created or left without a line — and it is the only place where you can reach them.

If two stations in the same production line share a zone, a warning is shown at the top of the line, naming the duplicated zone and the stations it is in.

**Deleting a station** asks what you mean:

- *Remove from this line* takes it out of that line only. The station stays, and if it was in no other line it moves to the *No production line* group.
- *Delete* removes the station from every line and loses its checklist. This cannot be undone.

### The station form

Station fields:

- **Name**: Simply a name.
- **Client ID**: Client ID of the station, usually from an external application that the client wants to link.
- **Machine station**: tick it if the station runs on a machine, then pick its **Machine setup**. For example: a Mobi One setup created in **Machine Settings**. Without it, the station is a manual station.
- **Enable when**: when the station is part of a panel's checklist: *Always*, *If Branch in Design*, *If Zone in Design* or *If Branch in Zone of Design*, using the **Branches** and **Zones** below.
- **Branches**: the branches the station looks for.
- **Zones (Assemblies)**: What zones are expected to be produced in this station. For example add 0 for a typical framing station.
- **Assembly Prefixes (Modules)**: the assembly prefixes the station works with, for module lines.
- **DWG Numbers Filter** and **Default DWG**: which drawings, by drawing number, the viewer shows at this station, and the one it opens first. Leave the filter empty to show them all.
- **Expected productivity**: the expected pace of the station, typed either as m²/min or as min/m²; the other value is filled in for you.

![The station form, with one checklist task](./station-form.svg)

1. The machine setup of a machine station.
2. When the task is included.
3. How often the task is included. Here: one checklist in every five.
4. What the worker has to add to complete the task.
5. When the station itself is part of a panel's checklist.

### Checklist tasks

As a last nested item, each station has a **Checklist**: the entries for the production users to check in the production interface ("the viewer"). **Add item** adds a task, and each task has an **Options** menu to move it up or down or delete it.

Checklist fields:

- **Task text**: The text that will be shown to the production user.
- **Branches** and **Zones**: used by *Enable when*.
- **Enable when**: when the task is included: *Always*, *If Branch in Design* (one of its branches is in the design), *If Zone in Design* (one of its zones is in the design) or *If Branch in Zone of Design* (one of its branches is in one of its zones). The station's own *Enable when* is checked first: a task of a station that is not enabled is never included.
- **QC Inclusion Criteria**: *All proofs* means every checklist gets this task. *1/n* adds it to 1 checklist every n checklists; *1/n randomized* does the same at a random pace. The count is kept per batch, and the first panel of a batch always gets the task.
- **DOCS**: A feature that allows the company to add documentation specific to the task, such as guidelines, specifications, ... Save the station first to upload them.
- **Require form**: the task asks for a form, which you design with the button next to it. **Expand this form as tasks in checklist** shows each field of the form as a task of its own.
- **QR field**: the task asks for a QR scan.
- **Require picture**: the task asks for a picture.

### The machine of a line

A line can name the machine it runs on. Tick **Line machine** in the line form and pick one.

There are two ways to record it, and both are fine:

- **On the line.** Use this when the line *is* one machine — a saw line, a plates cutter. There are no stations to hang it on.
- **On a single station.** Use this when the line has one station and the machine belongs to it. Nothing changes for the lines you already set up this way.

Either way, the machine's name appears on the line header, next to what the line builds. When it was read off a station rather than set on the line, it is shown in grey italics, so you can tell at a glance where it came from.

If a line has a machine **and** one of its stations has another one, the form says so. The line's machine is the one that counts for the line. It is a notice, not an error: the form saves either way.

A line with several stations that each have their own machine — an automated panel line — has no single machine to name. Give it one by creating an **H&M Mobi One V2 Production Line** machine setup and picking it as the line machine. That setup exists to hold what belongs to the whole line rather than to one of its tables; it has no settings yet, and each one will appear as it starts being used.

### Picking a machine setup

Both machine pickers — the one on a station and the one on a line — put the setups that usually go there first (under **Machine stations** or **Line machines**), and everything else under **Other machines**. Nothing is hidden: if you pick a setup from the second group, the form tells you where it normally goes and lets you carry on.

## Machine Settings

**Machine Settings** starts with two tiles, **New Machine setup** and **Import from JSON**. Below them, the setups are grouped: first one group per production line, with the setups that line runs; then *Not in any production line*, for station and line machines that nothing uses yet; then the rest by machine type. Licensed types (wood profiles cutters, wood plates saw cutters, Voortman and Valk) show how many setups you have out of your licensed maximum.

Each card shows the model, the file types it **Produces**, and **Used by**: the stations and production lines that use the setup. It warns only when a station or line machine is used by nothing. Its buttons edit, copy, download as JSON, and delete the setup.

When you create a machine setup, the **Model** list is grouped by where that kind of machine goes:

- **Production line settings** — holds what belongs to a whole line. Today that is *H&M Mobi One V2 Production Line*.
- **Machine stations** — goes on a station of a line.
- **Standalone machines** — machines you send generated files to: saws, cutters, profilers. These can also be named as the machine of a logistics line.

The setup window has a **General** tab (name, model, and what the model is: provider, where it attaches, and what it produces), and depending on the model a **Machine file** tab, a **Machine setup** tab with the machine settings, and one tab per file type it produces, holding the default job options for that file.

Most models have no settings of their own: a cutter is configured by the options of the file it is sent, not by a form here. When that is the case the General tab says so instead of showing you an empty form.

![Machine Settings](./machine-settings.svg)

1. One group per production line, with the setups that line runs.
2. **Used by**: the stations and lines that use the setup.
3. A station setup that nothing uses.
4. A licensed type: setups in use out of your licensed maximum.

### The machine configuration file

Some machine models accept the machine's own configuration file (XML or INI), in the **Machine file** tab. Uploading it fills the **Parsed params**, shown next to the uploader as read-only JSON: the top level is open and each block can be expanded. The **Current machine file** card shows the file name and when it was parsed, so you always know how old the configuration is.

## Automations

The Automations view holds the **Webhooks**, which send production events to external systems, and two things that work together: the **setups**, which say *how* something is generated, and the **action triggers**, which say *when*.

### Machine file setups

A machine file setup is a saved MOB v2 setup: how the machine file is built — operations, nailing, shifts and layers.

Running one takes a panel design, builds the machine file for **every station of every production line**, and sends it to the machines. There is no report and no download in between, and there is no way to limit it to a single line.

You use a machine file setup from two places:

- an **action trigger**, so it runs on its own, and
- the **AUTO MOB v2** file type, to run it by hand on the panels you pick.

### Drawing setups

A drawing setup is a saved set of drawings. It decides:

- **Views to generate** — front, top and section by default; back, bottom and right can be added.
- **Positioning origin** — where the parts are placed from.
- **One drawing per zone** — on by default. An extra drawing per zone of the panel, with the parts of the other zones drawn as a dashed outline. **View used for the zone drawings** picks its direction (front by default).
- **Include the framework (zone 0)** — on by default. The woods-only layer, drawn as FRAMEWORK.

Running one takes a design and writes the drawings straight into the design's files, marked as generated. There is no report in between.

You use a drawing setup from two places:

- an **action trigger**, so it runs on its own, and
- the **Launch action** button on the designs and multipanel groups tables, to run it by hand. Here the setup is optional: without one you get the default views (front, top, section, plus one per zone).

The design's drawings card shows whether a run is working or failed, and warns when a newer IFC arrived after the drawings were made, marking the outdated ones. **Generate the drawings again** from the same button; **Clean** deletes the generated ones without touching the drawings you uploaded yourself.

Each setup table has a **Used by** column naming the action triggers that use the setup. Deleting a setup also deletes the triggers that use it; the delete dialog lists them first.

### Action triggers

An action trigger runs something on its own when an event happens in production, with nobody clicking anything. Besides a name, it reads as three steps:

1. **When this happens** — the event. Today the only event is *A design finishes its analysis*.
2. **Only if** — an optional condition on a field of the design (`name`, `tipo`, or a key of its client data), matched as a full word, a prefix, or "contains". Leave it empty and the trigger applies to every design.
3. **Then do this** — the action, and the setup it runs with:
   - *Generate MOB v2 files and send them to the machines*, with a machine file setup.
   - *Generate the drawings of the design*, with a drawing setup — or none, for the default views.

In the table, a MOB trigger with no setup is marked *No setup picked*, and a drawings trigger with no setup is marked *Default views*.

![The action trigger form](./action-trigger.svg)

1. *Only if*: here, only designs whose `tipo` starts with `W`.
2. The setup the action runs with.

::: warning
A trigger runs for **every** design that matches, each time it finishes its analysis. Use *Only if* to narrow it down before turning one on in a busy project.
:::

pages.title: Multipanel Groups
pages.body:
# Multipanel Groups

Multipanel Groups let you combine multiple wall panels into a single unit that is processed together through the machine. This is a production-level decision — you create groups inside a batch to tell the machine to feed several panels consecutively as one run.

When a group is **valid**, the report system treats the whole group as a single logical panel: Bill of Materials reports use the combined rail length, and machine files (MOB2) are generated as one file for the whole group.

::: info Feature flag
Multipanel Groups must be enabled on your company by a Produuz.it administrator. Once enabled, a **Multipanel Groups** entry appears in each project's menu, and admins get a **Multipanel Configurations** table in **Projects Settings**.
:::

[[toc]]

## Configuration

The constraints for groups are kept in **multipanel configurations**, shared by the whole company. An admin manages them in **Projects Settings → Multipanel Configurations**: click **New** to add one, or the pencil to edit it. A company can have several, for example one per machine.

| Setting | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| **Name** | Name of the configuration. |
| **Default for new projects** | New projects use this configuration. |
| **Min. height (mm)** | Minimum panel height allowed in a group. |
| **Min. / Max. element width (mm)** | Allowed width range for individual panels. |
| **Max. transport width (mm)** | The combined width of all panels plus gaps must not exceed this value. This is typically the physical limit of the machine or transport system. |
| **Min. / Max. elements per group** | Minimum and maximum number of panels per group. |
| **Default gap (mm)** | Default gap between elements when creating a new group. |

Each project picks the configuration it uses in **Project Settings → Multipanel Config**.

## Creating a Group

Open **Multipanel Groups** in the project menu, choose a **Batch**, and click the **Multipanel** button in the table toolbar. The dialog has two sides:

1. **Select panels** (left) — tick two or more assemblies of the batch. Once a panel is selected, incompatible panels (different height or rail profile) are disabled; hover one to see why.
2. **Gaps between panels** (right) — set the gap between each pair of adjacent panels, in mm.
3. **Validation** — the checks run on their own every time the selection or a gap changes. Each requirement shows a pass or fail icon with a detail message.
4. **Group name** — give the group a name and click **Create**.

**Create** is only enabled when every check passes, so a new group is always saved as **valid**. Use the pencil on a row to edit a group, and **Update** to save it.

## Validation Requirements

All 7 requirements must pass before a group can be created.

| # | Requirement | What is checked |
|---|-------------|-----------------|
| 1 | **Height equality** | All panels must have the same height; each must meet the configured minimum. |
| 2 | **Element width & transport width** | Each panel's width must be within the configured [min, max] range, and the total width must not exceed the maximum transport width. |
| 3 | **Element count** | The number of panels must be within the configured minimum and maximum. |
| 4 | **Top/bottom rail framing** | Top and bottom rail profiles must be identical across all panels. |
| 5 | **Same batch** | All panels must belong to the same batch. |
| 6 | **Identical zones** | The zones checked by the configuration must be present in all panels or in none, with the same branches in each. |
| 7 | **Gap & total transport width** | Total combined width (sum of panel widths + all gaps) must not exceed the configured maximum. |

Saw and milling operations on the panel layer must also be equal across all panels. That is checked when the machine file is generated, not when the group is created.

## Group Status

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `draft` | Not validated yet. |
| `valid` | All validation checks passed. Reports and machine files treat the group as a single panel. |
| `invalid` | One or more validation checks failed. |

The **Valid** column of the table shows the result of the last validation; hover it for the details of each check. Click the refresh icon on a row to run the validation again, for example after a design change.

## Report Form — Assembly Selector

When building a report (BoM, machine files, etc.), the assembly selector is aware of multipanel groups:

- Each assembly that belongs to a group shows a **chip** with the group name and the panel count (e.g. `Group A ×3`). This makes it easy to spot which assemblies are part of a combined unit.
- A **Force multipanel selection** switch, on by default, sits above the selector. When it is on, selecting any assembly in a group automatically selects all the other assemblies of the same group. This prevents accidentally generating a report for only part of a group.

A group is only treated as one panel when **all** of its panels are in the selection. If only some are selected, each of them is handled as an individual panel.

## Bill of Materials Impact

When generating a BoM report (Wood BoM, Plates BoM, etc.) that includes all the assemblies of a **valid** Multipanel Group:

- The top rail and bottom rail parts are replaced by a single virtual part spanning the full group width.
- The rail **length** in the cut list equals `sum of all panel widths + sum of all gaps between panels`.
- All other part properties (material, profile, finish, etc.) are taken from the first panel's rail.
- Non-rail parts from each panel appear individually in the list, as usual.
- Only one row appears per rail category (one top rail, one bottom rail) for the entire group — not one per panel.

This ensures the cut list reflects the actual piece that goes through the machine, rather than individual per-panel lengths that would be incorrect.

::: tip Example
Two panels: 1200 mm and 900 mm wide, with a 10 mm gap between them.
Combined rail length = 1200 + 900 + 10 = **2110 mm**.
The BoM shows one top rail and one bottom rail, each 2110 mm long.
:::

## Machine File Impact (MOB2)

When generating a MOB2 machine file for a selection that includes all the assemblies of a **valid** Multipanel Group:

- A **single `.mob2` file** is generated for the entire group, named after the group.
- The file is placed in the batch folder as `<phase>/<batch>/<group_name>.mob2`.
- Part positions within the combined file are offset correctly: parts from panel 2 are placed after panel 1, with the configured gap applied — so the machine sees the full combined run in the correct order.
- The revision field is left blank for group files (since a group has no single design revision).

## Tracking Production Progress

Both the left-menu list (in the 3D viewer) and the **Multipanel Groups** management table show a row of small **station chips** for each group. Each chip represents one station of the batch's production line and shows how many panels of the group are ready at that station, in the form `ready/total`:

- An **outlined** chip means no panel has started the station yet.
- A **filled orange** chip means some panels are working there or are already ready there.
- A **filled green** chip means every panel of the group has been marked ready at that station.
- When every station of every panel is ready, a single **Ready** chip replaces the row.

Stations that none of the panels pass through are left out. Hover any chip to see the full breakdown — number of panels that are ready, currently working, and still waiting at that station.

In the viewer, open the group row to work on all its panels at once with the [Multiwall Checklist](/guide/viewer/#multiwall-checklist).

## Clearing Proofs in Bulk

In the **Multipanel Groups** management table, ticking the checkbox of one or more rows reveals a **Proof Options** menu in the toolbar. The **Clear proof** action wipes all production proofs for every panel of the selected groups in one operation — useful when a group needs to be reworked from the start. The same menu also offers **Set Ready** and **Merge checklist**, mirroring the actions available on individual constructibles. Next to it, **Launch action** generates the drawings of the selected groups.

pages.title: IFC Parsing Setup
pages.body:
# IFC Parsing Setup (IFC PS)

::: info Why this exists
The IFC standard is open and versatile, and every BIM application exports it in
its own way. What one exporter calls `REFERENCE` another writes as a property
set value, and a stud can be recognised by its name in one file and by its
profile in the next. An IFC Parsing Setup is how you tell produuz.it to read
**your** files.
:::

A company can have several setups, and **each project uses one**. Open them in
**Projects Settings → IFC Parsing Setups**, in the company menu under
**Settings**.

Every setting has a help button (**?**) that opens the help panel on the right,
with the same explanation you find here plus a typical example. The panel
follows whatever you pressed last, so you can leave it open while you work.

::: tip Let Claude write it for you
Building a setup from scratch is the slowest part of onboarding, and it is what
the **Claude connector** is most useful for. Give Claude the property list of a
few elements from your BIM application, describe your panels in your own words,
and ask it for the setup. It writes a JSON file you upload with the **UPLOAD**
button, and you check it tab by tab before saving.

See: [The setup file (JSON)](/guide/management/ifcps/json/) ·
[Claude connector (MCP)](/guide/mcp/)
:::

## How a setup is organised

The editor has seven tabs, in this order:

| Tab | What you set there |
| --- | ------------------ |
| [Hierarchy and project](#hierarchy-and-project) | How the file is split into modules and panels, where the names, phases and batches come from, and which assemblies are produced at all |
| [Custom part branches](#custom-part-branches) | Your own kinds of part beyond the built-in ones |
| [Panel part categories](#panel-part-categories) | Which elements are rails, studs, plates, bricks, openings and areas |
| [Steel cage part categories](#steel-cage-part-categories) | The same, for the steel cage flow |
| [Part properties](#part-properties) | Where each value of a part is read from |
| [Custom part classes](#custom-part-classes) | Kinds of part you tell apart inside a category, and what they do to the panel measurements |
| [Operations and machines](#operations-and-machines) | Which elements are nail lines, cuts and drills, and what the machine files read |

The filter box at the top left of each tab searches the settings by name, and
also by the values inside their rules, so typing `STIJL` lands on every rule
that uses it.

![The IFC Parsing Setup editor](./ifcps-editor.svg)

1. The seven tabs.
2. The filter, and the sections of the tab with how many settings each holds.
3. A setting with its rules, and its help button.
4. A rule: property, type of match and value. A part matches the setting when any one of its rules matches.
5. A rule that reads one property set only. See [Reading from a specific property set](#reading-from-a-specific-property-set).
6. The help panel. It follows the last help button you pressed.

## The two kinds of entry

Almost everything in a setup is one of two things.

### Rules

Used by categories, by the assembly filter and by the machine flags. Each rule
has three fields:

- **IFC Prop** — the property to look into.
- **Type of match** — *Match full word*, *Match prefix* or *Contains word*.
- **Value** — what to look for.

A part matches the setting when **any one** of its rules matches.

::: tip Example
Two rules on the *Top Rail Wood* category:

| IFC Prop  | Type of match | Value   |
| --------- | ------------- | ------- |
| REFERENCE | Match full word | TOPRAIL |
| REFERENCE | Match prefix    | TR      |

Parts with a `REFERENCE` of **TOPRAIL**, **TR**, **TR12** or **TR45** are top
rails. `TOPRAIL2`, `TOP_RAIL` and `12TR` are not.
:::

### Property names

Used by the properties. Here you only list the **IFC property names** that may
hold the value, in order of preference. The first one present on the element
wins.

::: tip Example
Two names on the *Zone (layer)* property, `WorkPlane` and `Layer`:

| Part | `WorkPlane` | `Layer`   | Detected zone |
| ---- | ----------- | --------- | ------------- |
| P1   | 1           | 2         | 1             |
| P2   | *(absent)*  | 3         | 3             |
| P3   | 1           | *(absent)* | 1            |
:::

::: warning Case does not matter
Property names and values are matched **case-insensitively**. `Reference`,
`REFERENCE` and `reference` are the same thing.
:::

### Reading from a specific property set

By default produuz.it looks for a property **anywhere in the element**: in any
of its property sets, and among the element's own attributes. That is what you
want almost always.

It becomes a problem when the same property name exists in two property sets
with different values — the exporter's `REFERENCE` and your own `REFERENCE`,
say. Then it is luck which one is read.

Every category rule, every filter and flag rule, and every property name has a
**Read from a specific property set** checkbox for that case. The rules of
custom part branches and custom part classes do not have it.

| Checkbox | Field | What is read |
| -------- | ----- | ------------ |
| unticked | — | The property wherever it appears. The normal case. |
| ticked | `Tekla_Common` | That property set only. Another set carrying a property of the same name is ignored. |
| ticked | *(left empty)* | The element's own attributes only: `name`, `ifc_tag`, `ifc_id`, `object_type`, `description`. |

Tick it when you have a reason to. An unticked entry behaves exactly as it
always has, and setups saved before this existed are untouched.

## Hierarchy and project

How the file is split, what the pieces are called, and which of them you
actually produce.

### Levels detection {#levels-detection}

Says how elements are grouped into modules, assemblies and subassemblies. Each
level has a **Detection system** and a **Value**: *By IFC class* (usually
`IfcElementAssembly`), *By part property*, for exporters that write no
containers at all, or *By assembly property*. The **Split full IFC** operation
works with *By IFC class* and *By part property* on the assembly level.

### Unit and project properties {#unit-and-project-properties}

*Levels detection* above says how a module and an assembly are recognised.
These say what is read from each one once it has been: what it is called, which
phase and batch it belongs to, and any extra values of yours that should travel
with it.

They are read off the **container** — the module or the assembly — and not off
its parts. Everything read off a part is in the
[Part properties](#part-properties) tab.

Leave one empty and produuz.it falls back to its own default, which for a name
is the container element's own name.

#### Module name {#module-name}

The properties holding the module design name, for example `Modulenummer`.
Instances of the same design share this value.

#### Module unit ID {#module-unit-id}

The properties holding the unique id of each module instance. Without it,
modules sharing a name are merged into one and you get a warning.

#### Assembly name {#assembly-name}

The properties holding the panel name. Left empty, the container's own name is
used.

#### Phase Name {#phase-name}

The property holding the phase a panel belongs to. Phases and batches are
created from these values when the file is split.

#### Batch Name {#batch-name}

The property holding the batch a panel belongs to.

#### Auto Parsed Client Meta {#auto-parsed-client-meta}

Properties copied onto the design as client data when the file is analysed.
Useful for anything of yours that has no field of its own.

### Assembly filter

A project file usually holds more than you produce: foundations, in-situ
concrete, the building next door. Two lists decide what the splitter takes out
of it.

#### Split only these assemblies {#split-only-these-assemblies}

Leave it empty and **every** assembly is split. With rules in it, only the
assemblies matching one of them are split out.

#### Never split these assemblies {#never-split-these-assemblies}

Assemblies matching one of these are never split out, **even when the first
list keeps them**. The drop list always wins, which is how you keep a whole
prefix and still leave a few names out of it.

An assembly that is not split leaves nothing behind: no IFC file, no design,
and nothing in the phase and batch counts.

::: details Example
*Split only these assemblies:* `ASSEMBLY_PREFIX` starts with `WA`

*Never split these assemblies:* `name` contains `_TEST`

You get every wall except the ones whose name carries `_TEST`. Roofs, floors
and everything else in the file are left alone.
:::

## Custom part branches {#custom-part-branches}

Branches are kinds of part beyond the built-in timber and plate: windows,
connectors, airtightness, electrical, plumbing.

Each branch has a name, its own rules, the geometry it **resembles** —
wood-like, plate-like or generic, so drawings, counts and cutting lists know
how to treat it — and two switches.

### Logistics enabled {#branch-logistics}

The parts of this branch reach the **parts list** and go through logistics.

### Counts in the panel measurements {#branch-in-metrics}

The parts of this branch take part in the panel **width, height, thickness and
surface**.

This exists because a branch is recognised *before* a part falls back to
timber, plate or steel from its category. A part your setup recognises
perfectly well as a window frame or a cladding profile can therefore have no
category at all, and a part with no category is outside every measurement —
which is why a panel can read thinner or smaller than it is, with no warning.

Leave it **off** for brackets, connectors and anything that sticks out past
the frame: counting those makes the panel read wider and taller than it is.
Turn it **on** for cladding, window frames and layers that are really part of
the panel.

::: info The measurements are not only a report figure
The **rack loads** are drawn from them. The width decides how many panels fit
in a rack row and the thickness how deep the stack builds, so a panel measured
short is a rack plan that does not fit on the floor.
See: [Delivery & Racks](/guide/logistics/delivery/)
:::

::: info It only decides whether the part takes part at all
Which measurements it is then left out of is a **custom part class** job. A
window frame that should set the thickness but add no surface gets the switch
here *and* a class with *Ignore in surface*. The branch says whether the part
participates; the class says what it is out of.
See: [Custom part classes](#custom-part-classes)
:::

::: info Both switches are off by default
Turning this on changes the measurements of every panel holding parts of that
branch, from its next analysis. Nothing moves until you tick it.
:::

## Panel part categories

The elements that make up a prefabricated panel. Every rule here matches the
**raw IFC properties** of the element — its Name, Reference, Material and the
rest, exactly as the modeller exported them.

### Frame

#### Top Rail Wood {#top-rail-wood}

The horizontal wood at the top of the frame. The studs are nailed into it from
above and the panel height is measured from its outer face.

#### Bottom Rail Wood {#bottom-rail-wood}

The horizontal wood at the bottom of the frame. The panel's zero height is its
outer face.

#### Extra Top Wood {#extra-top-wood}

Woods over the top rail, usually fitted after the studs are nailed.

#### Extra Bottom Wood {#extra-bottom-wood}

Woods below the bottom rail, usually fitted after the studs are nailed.

#### Wood profile {#wood-profile}

Any wood of the frame that is not a rail, a batten or an extra piece: the
studs, noggins and diagonals. This is the category the framing nail matrix
applies to.

#### Extra Frame Wood profile {#extra-frame-wood-profile}

Additional frame woods that are not part of the standard framing.

#### Wood Batten {#wood-batten}

Battens fixed on the panel.

### Plates

#### Plate {#plate}

A sheet fixed on a face of the frame: OSB, plasterboard, fibreboard. Its layer
decides the zone it is machined in.

#### Core Plate {#core-plate}

A plate inside the frame rather than on a face, such as a shear panel.

### Other parts

#### Bricks / Stones {#bricks-stones}

Single bricks or stones.

#### Opening {#opening}

Placeholders for doors and windows. They are not produced; they tell the
machines where the frame has a hole and give the reports their opening list.

### Areas and flags

Elements that are not produced but change how a panel is handled.

#### Lockout Area {#lockout-area}

Areas the machine must not work on.

#### Isolated Area {#isolated-area}

Areas that carry insulation.

#### Skip Framing Wood {#skip-framing-wood}

Parts that would fall into the frame by geometry but must not be counted as
framing wood.

::: info Hiding and ignoring a part are on the classes now
*Hidden Material* and *Ignored Part* used to be categories here. They never said
what a part **is**, they said how to treat it, so they are
[class behaviours](#class-behaviours) — *Ignore this part completely* and *Hide
in the 3D viewer*. Setups that had the old categories were moved across and
behave exactly as they did.

*Not Isolated Area* is gone too. Nothing ever read it.
:::

## Steel cage part categories

A secondary flow. Leave it empty if you do not produce steel cages.

#### Top Steel Profile {#top-steel-profile}

#### Bottom Steel Profile {#bottom-steel-profile}

#### Steel Profile {#steel-profile}

#### Steel Plate {#steel-plate}

#### Welding Seam {#welding-seam}

#### Compute holes {#compute-holes}

Whether the holes of the profile are computed for the machine file.

#### Assembly ID Level1 {#assembly-id-level1}

#### Assembly ID Level2 {#assembly-id-level2}

The two levels of assembly id of a steel cage.

## Part properties {#part-properties}

Where produuz.it reads each value of a part from. Each entry is a list of IFC
property names, tried in order.

### Identity

#### Part Name {#part-name}

The name produuz.it uses for the part, shown in the parts list, the reports and
the machine file templates.

Leave it empty and the part keeps the name the IFC element itself carries. Fill
it in when the useful name lives in a property set instead, for example
`ELEMENT_NAME` or `Beschrijving`.

- **The IFC name is always kept.** It stays visible in the part drawer, in the
  *Unknown parts* dialog of the viewer, and as its own optional column in the
  parts list.
- **It does not change how parts are classified.** The category and branch
  rules always match against the raw IFC properties. To match on the property
  you mapped here, add a rule on that property's own key.

#### Reference {#reference}
