An id expected to be the same across parts of the same shape. Usually
`reference` in Tekla Structures, and available in other exporters too.

#### Material Name {#material-name}

The material of the part.

#### Profile Name {#profile-name}

The name of the shaped section, for profiles that are not rectangular.

#### Profile Joined {#profile-joined}

Whether the profile is extended or joined to another one.

### Zone (layer) {#zone-layer}

The panel layer a part belongs to. `0` is the frame, and the layers on each
face are numbered outwards from it: `1`, `2` on one side and `-1`, `-2` on the
other.

Most IFC files write that layer with a letter instead of a sign, usually `F`
for the front face and `B` for the back one. produuz.it reads the letter: a
value holding a **`B`** becomes a negative zone, and anything else stays
positive.

| IFC value | Detected zone |
| --------- | ------------- |
| `F1`      | 1             |
| `F2`      | 2             |
| `B1`      | -1            |
| `B2`      | -2            |
| `Back2`   | -2            |
| `1`       | 1             |
| `-1`      | -1            |

Letters and other characters are stripped, so only the `B` changes the result.
A value that already carries a minus sign is used as it is.

::: warning
The `B` rule applies to every **numeric** property, not only the zone. Keep a
`B` out of the values you map to *Nail/Screw CTC*, *Mill/Saw depth*, *Isolation
order number* and *Tool ID*, because it would turn them negative.
:::

#### Positive side zones {#positive-side-zones}

#### Negative side zones {#negative-side-zones}

**BTLx only.** BTLx layer numbers come as plain numbers with no sign, so these
two rule lists declare which layers belong to each face of the panel.

### Details

#### Finish {#finish}

The finish of the part.

#### Comment {#comment}

A free comment shown with the part.

#### Weight (kg) {#weight-kg}

The weight of the part in kg. Some exporters write it in the element property
sets (`Weight`, `GEWICHT`), others export only the volume.

#### Volume (m3) {#volume-m3}

The volume of the part in m³. Exported by nearly every application, and what a
weight can be derived from when the exporter writes none.

#### Isolation order number {#isolation-order-number}

The order in which insulation areas are filled.

## Custom part classes {#custom-part-classes}

A **category** says what a part is: a stud, a rail, a plate. A **class** says
how your factory treats it. They are two different questions, and a part
answers both at once.

Classes are entirely your own. Nothing is built in and nothing is detected
automatically: a part is an I-beam only because a rule you wrote says so.

Give each class a name and add the rules that recognise it, with the same kind
of rule as the categories. A part can match several classes. Its **name** is
the first class in the list whose rules match, so put the more specific classes
first. Its **behaviours** add up from every class it matches. A part that
matches no class simply has none, and that is normal.

A class does two things.

**Its name** is what other settings look up when they behave differently per
kind of part — the framing nail matrix of the machine setups first of all.
See: [Mobi One](/guide/machine_files/machines/mobi_one/)

**Its behaviours** say what the class does to the panel measurements. That is
the *Behaviours* button on each class.

### Behaviours {#class-behaviours}

Every panel carries four measurements: its width, its height, its thickness and
its surface. By default every part counts in all four. A behaviour takes the
parts of one class out of one of them — or out of produuz.it altogether.

**Whole part**

| Behaviour | What it does |
| --------- | ------------ |
| Ignore this part completely | The part never reaches the parts list, the reports or the machine files. Use it for helper geometry, annotations and anything the modeller exported by accident. |
| Hide in the 3D viewer | The part is still measured and still produced, it is only not drawn. Use it for insulation, foils and fillers that would cover the frame. |

**Measurements**

| Behaviour | What it leaves the part out of |
| --------- | ------------------------------ |
| Ignore in surface | The net area, the gross area and the opening areas of the panel |
| Ignore in width (X) | The width of the panel |
| Ignore in height (Y) | The height of the panel |
| Ignore in thickness (Z) | The thickness of the panel |

They are all **off by default, and off means the part counts** — which is what
every part did before behaviours existed. Turning none on changes nothing.

::: info The measurements are not only a report figure
The **rack loads** are drawn from them. The width decides how many panels fit
in a rack row and the thickness how deep the stack builds, so a panel measured
short is a rack plan that does not fit on the floor.
See: [Delivery & Racks](/guide/logistics/delivery/)
:::

The four are separate because the measurements are separate, and that is what
makes the useful cases possible.

::: info Placeholder layers
The case behaviours were built for. Some modellers add a layer to a panel that
is not produced but occupies the space a real one will take — an insulation
layer, a finish, a service cavity.

That layer has to count for the **thickness**, because the panel really is that
thick. It must not count for the **surface**, because nothing was produced.

Give it a class, turn on *Ignore in surface*, *Ignore in width* and *Ignore in
height*, and leave *Ignore in thickness* **off**. The panel keeps its real
thickness and its surface stops counting a layer nobody built.
:::

::: info A part that sticks out
A bracket or an anchor that reaches past the edge of the panel makes it read
wider than it is. Give it a class and turn on *Ignore in width*, and only that
one. It still counts everywhere else.
:::

The class row shows what it ignores without opening anything, so a setup is
readable at a glance.

![A custom part class and its Behaviours dialog](./class-behaviours.svg)

1. The summary of what the class ignores.
2. **Behaviours** opens the dialog.
3. The surface: the net, gross and opening areas.
4. The three dimensions. For a placeholder layer, leave the thickness on.

::: info When the numbers change
Panel measurements are worked out during the **analysis** of a design, not when
you look at them. Saving the setup relaunches the analysis of the projects that
use it, and the new numbers appear when it finishes.

If your company has *Launch analysis automatically* turned off in the company
settings, nothing is relaunched and the old numbers stay until you launch the
analysis yourself.
:::

## Operations and machines

Nail lines, saw cuts, drills and glue are modelled as elements too. These rules
tell them apart from parts, and the properties below feed the machine files
directly.

::: info They are never measured
An operation says what a machine does, not what the panel is made of, so
nothing here counts towards the width, height, thickness or surface of a panel.
A saw mark that hangs below the bottom rail does not make the panel taller.
:::

### Operation lines

#### Frame Nail Lines {#frame-nail-lines}

A group of frame nails represented as a line. The line goes through the heads
of the nails.

#### Frame Nail Singles {#frame-nail-singles}

A single frame nail represented as a line. The line goes through the body of
the nail.

#### Plate Nail Lines {#plate-nail-lines}

The same as frame nail lines, for nails into the plates.

#### Plate Screw {#plate-screw}

Lines representing screws, read like the nail lines.

#### Glue lines {#glue-lines}

Glue lines, used for bricks.

#### Glue areas {#glue-areas}

Areas to be covered with glue.

### Cutting and milling

#### Frame Saw {#frame-saw}

Saw cuts on the frame.

#### Frame Drill {#frame-drill}

Drills on the frame.

#### Milling {#milling}

Milling lines.

#### Sawing {#sawing}

Sawing lines on the plates.

#### Drilling {#drilling}

Drilling operations.

### Machine parameters

#### Nail/Screw CTC {#nailscrew-ctc}

The centre-to-centre distance in nail and screw lines.

#### Mill/Saw depth {#millsaw-depth}

The depth of a milling or sawing line.

#### Tool ID for mob2 nailing {#tool-id-for-mob2-nailing}

The tool the MOB2 machine must use for the nailing.

#### Frame Saw Size {#frame-saw-size}

The side of the frame the saw works on.

#### Brick Type {#brick-type}

The type of the brick.

### Machine flags

Each of these has an IFC property and, beside it, a BTLx rule list that does
the same job for BTLx files.

#### Bricks: Machine Flag {#bricks-machine-flag}

#### Bricks: Machine Flag (BTLx) {#bricks-machine-flag-btlx}

A brick that is machine built rather than laid by hand.

#### Isolation: Machine Flag {#isolation-machine-flag}

#### Isolation: Machine Flag (BTLx) {#isolation-machine-flag-btlx}

Insulation applied by the machine.

#### Battens: Machine Flag {#battens-machine-flag}

#### Battens: Machine Flag (BTLx) {#battens-machine-flag-btlx}

Battens fitted by the machine.

#### Milling: V-Mill {#milling-v-mill}

#### Milling: V-Mill (BTLx) {#milling-v-mill-btlx}

A milling line that must be done as a V-mill.

::: info Skip Framing Wood is on the other tab
It follows the same pattern — one IFC property and one BTLx rule list beside it
— but it sits with the areas and flags, on
[Panel part categories](#skip-framing-wood).
:::

## BTLx files

BTLx files are read with the same setup, with two differences:

- **No property sets.** BTLx parts carry plain attributes, so the *Read from a
  specific property set* checkbox is not offered on the BTLx rules, and a rule
  that names a property set never matches a BTLx part.
- **Zones need declaring.** BTLx layer numbers have no sign, so the face of the
  panel comes from the [Positive side zones](#positive-side-zones) and
  [Negative side zones](#negative-side-zones) rules instead of from a letter.

The settings that are BTLx-only are marked with a **BTLx** chip in the editor.

## Saving

The setup is validated before it is saved. If something is missing — a rule
with an empty value, typically — you get a message and the editor opens the tab
holding the offending field and scrolls to it.

::: warning Saving relaunches the analysis
Saving a setup used by projects relaunches their analysis, so the parts are
re-read with the new rules. The editor warns you before it does and lists the
projects affected. There you can choose **Save As Clone** to keep the projects
on the old setup, or save without launching the analysis.
:::

## Moving a setup around

The **↓** button on a setup row downloads it as a JSON file, and **UPLOAD** in
the toolbar reads one back in. That is how you copy a setup between companies,
keep a version outside the platform, or have Claude write one for you.

![The IFC Parsing Setups card](./ifcps-setups.svg)

1. **UPLOAD** reads a setup file in.
2. The default setup of the company.
3. How many projects use the setup. Hover it to see which.
4. The row actions: edit, download (↓), clone, lock and delete.

Uploading saves nothing on its own: the file opens in this same editor, and it
exists when you press Save.

See: [The setup file (JSON)](/guide/management/ifcps/json/)

pages.title: The setup file (JSON)
pages.body:
# The setup file (JSON)

A parsing setup can be **downloaded as a JSON file and uploaded back**. The file
holds every rule of the setup, so it is how you move a setup between companies,
keep a copy outside the platform, or write a setup somewhere else and bring it
in finished.

This page is the reference for that file: every field, every key, and what a
value has to look like for the platform to read it.

::: tip You do not have to write it by hand
Claude can write the whole file for you from a sample IFC and a description of
your panels. See [Let Claude write it](#let-claude-write-it) at the end of this
page.
:::

[[toc]]

## Download and upload

Both live in **Projects Settings → IFC Parsing Setups**, in the company menu
under **Settings**.

| Action | Where | What it does |
| ------ | ----- | ------------ |
| Download | The **↓** button on a setup row | Saves `ifcps_<name>.json`. The uuid and the company are stripped, so the file describes rules and nothing else. |
| Upload | **UPLOAD** in the toolbar | Reads the file and **opens the editor filled in with it**. |

Uploading saves nothing on its own. The file lands in the normal editor, you
check it tab by tab, and it exists only when you press **Save**.

::: warning A uuid in the file overwrites that setup
A downloaded file carries no `uuid`, so uploading it always creates a **new**
setup. If you add a `uuid` by hand, saving overwrites the setup with that uuid
and re-analyses every project using it. Leave it out.
:::

## The two building blocks

Almost every value in the file is one of two things.

### A rule

Used by the categories, the assembly filter, the machine flags, the branches and
the classes. Three keys:

```json
{ "prop_key": "reference", "match": "prefix", "value": "TR" }
```

| Key | Value |
| --- | ----- |
| `prop_key` | The property to look into. Any property name the file carries, or one of the five element attributes below. Case does not matter. |
| `match` | `"all"`, `"prefix"` or `"contains"`. |
| `value` | What to look for. Case does not matter. |

| `match` | Matches when the property value |
| ------- | ------------------------------- |
| `all` | is exactly this value |
| `prefix` | starts with this value |
| `contains` | holds this value anywhere |

A part matches a setting when **any one** of its rules matches. A rule whose
`prop_key` the element does not carry never matches, and neither does one whose
`match` is missing or misspelled.

::: danger Never leave `value` empty
An empty `value` with `match` set to `prefix` or `contains` matches **every**
element that carries the property, because every string starts with nothing and
holds nothing. A whole category would swallow the panel.

The editor refuses to save a rule with an empty value, so an uploaded file is
caught before it does any harm — but it is caught as a red field on some tab you
have to go and find. Do not write one.
:::

The five element attributes are always available as `prop_key`, whatever the
file's property sets are called:

`name` · `ifc_tag` · `ifc_id` · `object_type` · `description`

Everything else has to be a property the exporter actually wrote: `reference`,
`zone`, `profile` and the rest are only useful if your IFC carries a property
with that name.

### A property name list

Used by everything under `props`, `steel_props` and `project_props`. Here you do
not match, you say **where to read a value from**: a list of property names,
tried in order, first one present on the element wins.

```json
"weight": ["WEIGHT", "GEWICHT"]
```

### Reading from one property set only

Both blocks take an optional `pset`, for the case where two property sets carry
the same property name with different values.

```json
{ "prop_key": "reference", "match": "prefix", "value": "TR", "pset": "Tekla_Common" }
{ "key": "ZONE", "pset": "Pset_WallCommon" }
```

| `pset` | What is read |
| ------ | ------------ |
| absent | The property wherever it appears. The normal case. |
| `"Tekla_Common"` | That property set only. |
| `""` | The element's own attributes only. |

A property name list takes the plain string form `"ZONE"` or the scoped form
`{"key": "ZONE", "pset": "..."}`, and you can mix both in the same list.

The editor offers `pset` on the category, filter and flag rules and on the
property names. It is not offered on the entries of `custom_branches` and
`part_classes`, so leave it out there.

::: info BTLx files have no property sets
The same setup reads BTLx files, where `prop_key` is the name of an attribute on
the BTLx part (`Designation`, `Material`, `Group`). A scoped entry never matches
a BTLx part.
:::

## Top-level fields

```json
{
  "name": "Tekla Wall Panels",
  "is_default": false,
  "setup": {},
  "props": {},
  "steel_setup": {},
  "steel_props": {},
  "project_setup": {},
  "project_props": {},
  "level_setup": {},
  "custom_branches": [],
  "part_classes": []
}
```

| Field | Type | Holds |
| ----- | ---- | ----- |
| `name` | string, **max 22 characters** | The setup name. Required. |
| `is_default` | boolean | Whether new projects start from this setup. Only one setup per company can be the default. |
| `setup` | object | Panel part categories, operations and machine flags. Rule lists. |
| `props` | object | Part properties. Property name lists. |
| `steel_setup` | object | Steel cage categories. Rule lists. |
| `steel_props` | object | Steel cage properties. Property name lists. |
| `project_setup` | object | The assembly filter. Rule lists. |
| `project_props` | object | What is read off a module or an assembly. Property name lists. |
| `level_setup` | object | How the file is split into levels, plus the BTLx zone rules. |
| `custom_branches` | array | Your own kinds of part. |
| `part_classes` | array | Your own classes and their behaviours. |

Every one of them may be left out, and an empty object or list is valid. A
category with no rules simply recognises nothing.

::: details Fields you can ignore
`wood_setup`, `wood_props`, `concrete_setup`, `concrete_props`, `custom_setup`,
`custom_props` and `level_props` exist in the file for compatibility. The editor
writes to none of them. Leave them out.

`read_only` and `company_lock` are locks, not rules. Leave them out too.
:::

## `setup` — categories, operations and flags

Every key holds a **list of rules**.

::: danger A mistyped key here is not ignored
The rules under it still run, and a part matching one is filed under a category
nothing recognises: it drops out of the parts list, the measurements, the reports
and the machine files without a word. It can also **outrank a correct rule** and
take a part away from the category it belonged in.

Check every key against the tables below. This is the single most common way a
hand-written setup goes wrong.
:::

### Frame

| Key | What it is |
| --- | ---------- |
| `top_rail` | The horizontal wood at the top of the frame |
| `bottom_rail` | The horizontal wood at the bottom |
| `extra_top_rail` | Woods over the top rail |
| `extra_bottom_rail` | Woods below the bottom rail |
| `wood` | Any other frame wood: studs, noggins, diagonals |
| `extra_wood` | Frame woods outside the standard framing |
| `batten` | Battens fixed on the panel |

### Plates

| Key | What it is |
| --- | ---------- |
| `plate` | A sheet on a face of the frame |
| `core_plate` | A plate inside the frame |

### Other parts

| Key | What it is |
| --- | ---------- |
| `brick` | Single bricks or stones |
| `opening` | Door and window placeholders, not produced |

### Areas and flags

| Key | What it is |
| --- | ---------- |
| `lockout_area` | Areas the machine must not work on |
| `isolated_area` | Areas that carry insulation |
| `skip_framing_wood` | BTLx parts that must not be counted as framing wood |

### Operation lines

| Key | What it is |
| --- | ---------- |
| `frame_nail` | Frame nail lines |
| `frame_nail_single` | Single frame nails |
| `plate_nail` | Plate nail lines |
| `plate_screw` | Plate screws |
| `glue` | Glue lines |
| `glue_area` | Glue areas |

### Cutting and milling

| Key | What it is |
| --- | ---------- |
| `frame_saw` | Saw cuts on the frame |
| `frame_drill` | Drills on the frame |
| `milling` | Milling lines |
| `sawing` | Sawing lines on the plates |
| `drilling` | Drilling operations |

### Machine flags (BTLx)

Each one mirrors a property of the same job under `props`, for files that carry
attributes instead of properties.

| Key | What it is |
| --- | ---------- |
| `brick_machine_flag` | Bricks built by the machine |
| `isolation_machine_flag` | Insulation applied by the machine |
| `battens_machine_flag` | Battens fitted by the machine |
| `v_mill` | Milling lines done as a V-mill |

::: info Two keys that used to live here
`ignore_me` and `hidden_material` were categories and are now **class
behaviours** — `skip_everything` and `hide_in_viewer` on a
[part class](#part-classes). A setup written today should use the classes; old
files keep working. `not_isolated_area` was never read by anything.
:::

## `props` — part properties

Every key holds a **list of property names**. Unlike `setup`, a key that is not
in this table is read by nothing — silently, so the property simply comes out
empty and nothing says why.

| Key | What it reads |
| --- | ------------- |
| `name` | The part name. Left out, the element's own Name is used. |
| `fab_ref` | The reference, expected to be the same for parts of the same shape |
| `material` | The material name |
| `shaped_section_name` | The profile name, for sections that are not rectangular |
| `profile_joined` | Whether the profile is extended or joined |
| `zone` | The panel layer the part belongs to |
| `finish` | The finish |
| `comment` | A free comment |
| `weight` | The weight in kg |
| `volume` | The volume in m³ |
| `isolation_order` | The order insulation areas are filled in |
| `nail_ctc` | Centre-to-centre distance in nail and screw lines |
| `mill_depth` | Depth of a milling or sawing line |
| `nail_tool_id` | The tool the MOB2 machine nails with |
| `frame_saw_side` | The side of the frame the saw works on |
| `brick_type` | The type of brick |
| `is_machine_brick` | Bricks built by the machine |
| `is_machine_isolation` | Insulation applied by the machine |
| `is_machine_battens` | Battens fitted by the machine |
| `is_vmill` | Milling lines done as a V-mill |
| `skip_framing_wood` | Parts not to be counted as framing wood |

::: warning The zone reads a letter as a sign
A zone value holding a **`B`** becomes a negative zone; anything else stays
positive, and letters are stripped. So `F1` is `1` and `B2` is `-2`.

That rule applies to **every numeric property**, so keep a `B` out of the values
you map to `nail_ctc`, `mill_depth`, `isolation_order` and `nail_tool_id`.
:::

## `steel_setup` and `steel_props`

Only for the steel cage flow. Leave both out if you do not produce steel cages.

| `steel_setup` key | What it is |
| ----------------- | ---------- |
| `top_steel_rail` | Top steel profile |
| `bottom_steel_rail` | Bottom steel profile |
| `steel_profile` | Any other steel profile |
| `steel_plate` | Steel plate |
| `steel_welding_seam` | Welding seam |

| `steel_props` key | What it reads |
| ----------------- | ------------- |
| `steel_compute_holes` | Whether the holes of the profile are computed |
| `assembly_id` | Assembly id, level 1 |
| `assembly_id2` | Assembly id, level 2 |

## `project_props` — read off a module or an assembly

Property name lists, read off the **container**, not off its parts.

| Key | What it reads |
| --- | ------------- |
| `module_design_name` | The module design name. Instances of the same design share it. |
| `custom_module_id` | The unique id of each module instance |
| `assembly_design_name` | The panel name. Left out, the container's own name is used. |
| `phase_name` | The phase a panel belongs to |
| `batch_name` | The batch a panel belongs to |
| `client_meta` | Properties copied onto the design as client data |

## `project_setup` — the assembly filter

Two rule lists deciding which assemblies are split out of the project file.

```json
"project_setup": {
  "assembly_filter":     [{"prop_key": "ASSEMBLY_PREFIX", "match": "prefix", "value": "WA"}],
  "assembly_filter_out": [{"prop_key": "name", "match": "contains", "value": "_TEST"}]
}
```

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | ------- |
| `assembly_filter` | Empty or absent, every assembly is split. With rules, **only** matching assemblies are split. |
| `assembly_filter_out` | Matching assemblies are never split, even when the first list keeps them. |

The drop list always wins. An assembly that is not split produces nothing: no
IFC file, no design, no row in the phase and batch counts.

## `level_setup` — how the file is split

Three levels, each an object rather than a list of rules.

```json
"level_setup": {
  "module":      { "detection": "ifc_class", "match": "IfcElementAssembly" },
  "assembly":    { "detection": "ifc_class", "match": "IfcElementAssembly" },
  "subassembly": { "detection": "part_prop", "match": "SUBASSEMBLY" }
}
```

| `detection` | `match` is |
| ----------- | ---------- |
| `ifc_class` | An IFC class name: `IfcElementAssembly`, `IfcWall`, `IfcSlab`, `IfcPresentationLayerAssignment` |
| `part_prop` | A property name read off the parts |
| `ass_prop` | A property name read off the assembly |

The same object also holds two more keys, each a plain **list of rules**, because
BTLx layer numbers carry no sign and the face of the panel has to be declared.

| Key | What it is |
| --- | ---------- |
| `positive_zone` | BTLx layers on the reference face of the panel |
| `negative_zone` | BTLx layers on the opposite face |

```json
"positive_zone": [{"prop_key": "Layer", "match": "all", "value": "1"}],
"negative_zone": [{"prop_key": "Layer", "match": "all", "value": "2"}]
```

They do nothing for IFC files, where the zone sign comes from the `zone`
property instead.

## `custom_branches`

Kinds of part beyond the built-in timber and plate: windows, connectors,
airtightness, electrical, plumbing.

```json
"custom_branches": [
  {
    "name": "windows",
    "alike": "generic",
    "logistics": true,
    "metrics": true,
    "entries": [{"prop_key": "reference", "match": "prefix", "value": "WIN"}]
  }
]
```

| Key | Value |
| --- | ----- |
| `name` | The branch name. Lowercased everywhere it is used. |
| `alike` | `"generic"`, `"plate"` or `"wood"` — the geometry it resembles, so drawings and cutting lists know how to treat it. |
| `logistics` | `true` puts its parts in the parts list and through logistics. Default `false`. |
| `metrics` | `true` counts its parts in the panel width, height, thickness and surface. Default `false`. |
| `entries` | The rules that recognise it. |

::: warning `metrics` is off by default and that has consequences
A branch is recognised **before** a part falls back to timber or plate from its
category, so a part your setup knows perfectly well can end up with no category
— and a part with no category is outside every panel measurement.

Turn `metrics` on for cladding and window frames. Leave it off for brackets and
anything that sticks out past the frame.
:::

## `part_classes`

A category says what a part is. A class says how your factory treats it. A part
can match several classes. Its name is the **first class in the list whose rules
match**, so put the more specific classes first. Its behaviours add up from every
class it matches.

```json
"part_classes": [
  {
    "name": "Placeholder",
    "entries": [{"prop_key": "name", "match": "prefix", "value": "PLH"}],
    "behaviours": {"skip_area": true, "skip_x": true, "skip_y": true}
  }
]
```

| Key | Value |
| --- | ----- |
| `name` | The class name. Settings that behave differently per kind of part, the framing nail matrix first, look it up by this. |
| `entries` | The rules that recognise it. |
| `behaviours` | Optional. Absent means the part behaves normally. |

| Behaviour | What it does |
| --------- | ------------ |
| `skip_area` | The part is left out of the net, gross and opening areas |
| `skip_x` | Left out of the panel width |
| `skip_y` | Left out of the panel height |
| `skip_z` | Left out of the panel thickness |
| `skip_everything` | The part is ignored completely: no parts list, no reports, no machine files |
| `hide_in_viewer` | Still measured and still produced, only not drawn in the 3D viewer |

All of them are `false` when absent, and `false` means the part counts. Only the
keys you turn on need to be in the file.

::: info The placeholder case
A layer that is not produced but takes up the space a real one will: it has to
count for the **thickness**, because the panel really is that thick, and not for
the **surface**, because nothing was produced. Turn on `skip_area`, `skip_x` and
`skip_y`, and leave `skip_z` off. That is the example above.
:::

## A complete example

A small but working setup. Every field it leaves out is simply not used.

```json
{
  "name": "Tekla Wall Panels",
  "level_setup": {
    "module":   { "detection": "ifc_class", "match": "IfcElementAssembly" },
    "assembly": { "detection": "ifc_class", "match": "IfcElementAssembly" }
  },
  "project_props": {
    "assembly_design_name": ["ASSEMBLY_NAME"],
    "phase_name": ["PHASE"],
    "batch_name": ["BATCH"]
  },
  "project_setup": {
    "assembly_filter_out": [
      { "prop_key": "name", "match": "contains", "value": "_TEST" }
    ]
  },
  "setup": {
    "top_rail": [
      { "prop_key": "reference", "match": "all", "value": "TOPRAIL" },
      { "prop_key": "reference", "match": "prefix", "value": "TR" }
    ],
    "bottom_rail": [
      { "prop_key": "reference", "match": "prefix", "value": "BR" }
    ],
    "wood": [
      { "prop_key": "reference", "match": "prefix", "value": "W" }
    ],
    "plate": [
      { "prop_key": "reference", "match": "prefix", "value": "P" }
    ],
    "opening": [
      { "prop_key": "name", "match": "contains", "value": "OPENING" }
    ],
    "frame_nail": [
      { "prop_key": "name", "match": "prefix", "value": "FNL" }
    ]
  },
  "props": {
    "fab_ref": ["REFERENCE"],
    "zone": ["ZONE", "LAYER"],
    "material": ["MATERIAL"],
    "weight": ["WEIGHT", "GEWICHT"],
    "volume": ["VOLUME", "NETVOLUME"],
    "nail_ctc": ["NAIL_CTC", "SCREW_CTC"]
  },
  "custom_branches": [
    {
      "name": "windows",
      "alike": "generic",
      "logistics": true,
      "metrics": true,
      "entries": [
        { "prop_key": "reference", "match": "prefix", "value": "WIN" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "part_classes": [
    {
      "name": "Placeholder",
      "entries": [
        { "prop_key": "name", "match": "prefix", "value": "PLH" }
      ],
      "behaviours": { "skip_area": true, "skip_x": true, "skip_y": true }
    }
  ]
}
```

## Before you upload

- `name` is present and **22 characters or fewer**.
- There is no `uuid`.
- Every key is one from the tables above. A mistyped key under `props` is read by
  nothing; a mistyped key under `setup` is worse, because its rules still run.
- Every rule has all three of `prop_key`, `match` and `value`, and `match` is one
  of `all`, `prefix`, `contains`. A misspelled `match` never matches anything.
- No rule has an empty `value`. The editor refuses to save one, and with
  `prefix` or `contains` it would have matched everything.
- Every `prop_key` and every property name is a property your IFC really carries.
  This is the one thing the file cannot tell you: check it against a sample file.

After uploading, walk the tabs before saving. The editor is the same one you
would have filled in by hand, and it validates the same way.

## Let Claude write it

produuz.it has a **Claude connector**, and writing a parsing setup is what it is
most useful for. Claude can read this documentation, so it knows every key on
this page and what each one is for.

Add the connector — see [Claude connector (MCP)](/guide/mcp/) — and then:

1. **Give it your properties.** Export the property list of a few elements from
   your BIM application — one stud, one rail, one plate, one panel — and paste it
   in. That list is what nearly every rule is written from.
2. **Describe your panels** in your own words: what marks a top rail, what marks
   a plate, which elements are not produced, where the phase and the batch come
   from.
3. **Ask for the file.** For example:

   > *Write me an IFC parsing setup JSON for produuz.it. Here are the properties
   > of four elements from our Tekla export. Top rails have REFERENCE starting
   > with TR, studs W, plates P. The phase is in the PHASE property of the
   > assembly. We do not produce steel cages.*

4. **Upload it** with the UPLOAD button and check every tab before saving.

Claude can also read a setup you already have. Download it, paste it in, and ask
why a part is landing in the wrong category or which rules are never used.

### Or let it create the setup directly

If you are a company administrator, Claude can skip the file and put the setup
straight into **Projects Settings → IFC Parsing Setups**. It asks for a separate
permission the first time, and you can say no and keep working with files.

What it creates is inert: no project uses it, nothing is re-analysed, and it cannot
touch a setup that already exists or make one the default. You still open it, walk
the tabs and assign it yourself. The checks on this page are not skipped either —
they are applied by the tool, so a key that is not in the tables above is refused
rather than stored.

See: [Creating a parsing setup](/guide/mcp/#creating-a-parsing-setup)

::: warning Always check what comes back
Claude cannot see your IFC file, only what you tell it about it. It writes the
rules; you check them against a real file. Nothing is saved until you press
**Save** in the editor, and the first real test is Step 9 of the
[setup tutorial](/tutorials/ifcps/): split a sample file and look for parts
landing in **unknown**.
:::

pages.title: Company Backup
pages.body:
# Company Backup

The backup feature lets company admins generate a full export of their company data for safekeeping.

## Generating a Backup

1. Go to **Company settings** (in the **Settings** section of the left menu, in company-wide mode).
2. On the company card, click **Company Backups**. Only company admins see this button.
3. Check the **email** address the download link is sent to. It is filled in with your own.
4. Choose what to include: **Include company data**, **Include users data** and **Include production lines data** are all ticked by default.
5. Pick the projects in **Select projects to include in backup**, or use the shortcut buttons: **ADD STDLIBS** (standard libraries), **ADD PROJECTS** (active projects), **ADD ARCHIVED** (archived projects), **ADD ALL**, and **Clean** to empty the list.
6. Click **Generate**.

::: info
Backups are generated in the background and can take some time, depending on the amount of data. When the backup is ready, you get an email with the download link, and the same link arrives as a message in the app.
:::

## What's Included

The backup is a single `.zip` file. Depending on what you ticked, it contains:

- **Company data**: the company record and its files (logos, banners), production events, company-level reports, webhooks, parsing setups, and the part batches and proofs that belong to no project.
- **Users data**: the user accounts of the company.
- **Production lines data**: production lines, stations, machine setups, action triggers and their setups, with their files (such as checklist docs).
- **Each selected project**: the project and its files, batches, designs, constructibles and parts with their files, issues, production proofs, part batches and reports.

pages.title: Mobfile Generator
pages.body:
# Mobfile Generator

The **Mobfile Generator** creates MOB v2 machine files from uploaded IFC, BTLx, BTL, JJS or WUP files, for a chosen production line and parsing setup, without going through the regular project flow.

You find it in the **Files** section of the company menu.

The screen has three parts: **Upload**, where you drop the files; **Settings**, where you pick the production line and the parsing setup, and adjust the job options of each machine station of that line; and the **Files** table, the tool's own job history with status, input/output files, and metadata. Press **Generate** to upload the files and start the job.

::: info License
The Mobfile Generator is gated by your company's modules. If the menu entry is greyed out, contact your administrator.
:::

pages.title: Production Planning
pages.body:
# Production Planning

The Production Planning view lets you schedule constructibles (assemblies and modules) on a calendar, manage production priorities, and visualize workload across your production lines.

Open it from **Production Overview** in the left menu. It needs the production management module.

[[toc]]

![The Production Planning calendar](./planning-calendar.svg)

1. The production line, the projects and the first month shown.
2. **Reload** and **Save changes**, enabled while there are unsaved changes. The cog opens the settings.
3. The constructibles with no date yet. Drag one onto a day.
4. The workload of the day. See [Workload](#workload).
5. The selected constructible: green.
6. A modified constructible, not saved yet: orange.
7. A constructible that is past its date and not ready: red.

## Calendar View

Pick a **production line** in the toolbar first: the calendar appears once a line is selected. It displays 1 to 4 months at a time, starting from the **Planning Month** chosen in the toolbar, with each day showing the constructibles of that line scheduled for production on that date. Items are ordered by priority within each day. Week numbers are shown next to each week.

### Visual Indicators

- **Green** — Selected constructible.
- **Orange** — Modified (unsaved changes).
- **Red** — Overdue (past scheduled date, not yet ready).
- **Grey** — Past dates, already ready.
- **Blue** — Normal scheduled item.

## Scheduling Constructibles

### Drag and Drop

Drag a constructible from one date to another to reschedule it. You can also drag items from the **Unscheduled constructibles** panel above the calendar into a date, or drag a scheduled item back onto that panel to remove its date. The panel is shown when **Show Unscheduled** is on in the settings.

### Priority

Within a single day, constructibles are produced in priority order (1 = first). Use the up/down arrows on a card to reorder items within a date.

### Day menu

Click a day number to open its menu:

- **Shift constructibles** — Move everything on that day to a new date. Two options: also shift the constructibles scheduled after that date by the same number of days, and count only the shown weekdays (so weekends can be skipped).
- **Day work capacity** — Set the work capacity of that date for the selected production line, in minutes. This is saved on the line and used by the workload bar.
- **Constructible sorting** — Reorder the constructibles of that day by dragging them, or sort them by design, by custom column or by project.

### Multi-Select

- **Ctrl+Click** — Select multiple individual items.
- **Shift+Click** — Select a range of items.

This allows you to move or modify several constructibles at once.

## Filters

- **Production line** — Show only constructibles assigned to a specific line. Required.
- **Projects** — Filter by one or more projects.
- **Planning Month** — The first month shown.

## Settings

Click the settings icon to configure the calendar display:

| Setting | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| **Months to show** | Show 1 to 4 months at a time. |
| **Calendar height** | Adjust the height of each month calendar. |
| **Show Unscheduled** | Show or hide the **Unscheduled constructibles** panel. |
| **Show Ready** | Show or hide constructibles that are already ready. |
| **Show workload** | Show a workload bar on each calendar date. |
| **Tweak PL work capacity** | Replace the line's daily capacity (minutes per date) while you plan. |
| **Shown Weekdays** | Choose which days of the week to display. |
| **Constructible fields** | Select which data to show on each card: design name, client order ID, project, superproject, UUID, status. |

These settings are remembered in your browser, except **Tweak PL work capacity**, which is cleared when you change the production line or reload the page.

## Workload

When **Show workload** is on, each calendar date shows a bar with a percentage: the total expected production time for that day compared to the production line's capacity. Hover the bar to see the expected time of each constructible, the total and the day capacity.

The bar is red up to 50 %, orange up to 90 %, green up to 100 % and blue above 100 % (overloaded).

The workload is calculated from:
- Design area (m²) of each scheduled constructible
- **Expected worktime** per m² of each station of the line that works on the design
- The line's **Worktime Capacity** (minutes per day), or the **Day work capacity** set for that date

::: tip
Use **Tweak PL work capacity** in the settings to try a different daily capacity (for example overtime or reduced shifts) without changing the line. Use **Day work capacity** in the day menu to store a different capacity for one date.
:::

## Saving Changes

After making scheduling changes, click **Save changes** to persist the updated dates and priorities. Unsaved changes are highlighted in orange. **Reload** discards them and loads the calendar again. Both buttons are active only while there are unsaved changes.

pages.title: Quantities
pages.body:
# Quantities / BoM Matrix

The Quantities view lets you plan how many of each design to produce across project phases and batches. It uses a matrix layout where you define quantities before generating the actual constructibles.

[[toc]]

![The Quantities matrix, in the batch view of a phase](./quantities-matrix.svg)

1. The axis (**Phases** or **Batches**, with the phase), and which designs to show.
2. Filter, add a column, sorting, the keyboard help and the **Bulk** menu.
3. The save state. See [Managing Quantities](#managing-quantities).
4. **Generate**, with what it would create and delete. See [Saved is not the same as generated](#saved-is-not-the-same-as-generated).
5. The status bar: target, assigned, area, and the rows that do not add up.
6. A batch column. The split icon means the batch has name prefixes.
7. **Assigned / target** of the design, with the button that balances the row.
8. The selected cell, with `−` and `+`.

## Matrix Layout

The matrix is organized as:

- **Rows** — Design names, grouped into modules and assemblies. Only the latest revision of each design is shown, plus any older revision that still has units in the project (its revision icon is red).
- **Columns** — Project phases (or batches, depending on the view).
- **Cells** — The quantity count for each design × phase combination.
- **Totals** — Row totals (all phases for a design) and column totals (all designs in a phase).

## View Modes

Two buttons in the toolbar switch the axis: **Phases** shows the project phases, **Batches** shows the batches of one phase, picked in the **Phase** selector beside them. The choice is kept in the address bar, so a reload or Back keeps you where you were, and a phase view can be bookmarked or shared.

Next to them, **All** / **Modules** / **Assemblies** chooses which designs are listed.

### Phase View

Shows a high-level summary with one column per project phase. Each cell shows the total quantity of a design across all batches in that phase.

### Batch View

Select a specific phase to drill down into its batches. Each column represents a batch, showing the detailed quantity breakdown.

## Managing Quantities

- **Edit cells** — The **−** / **+** buttons appear on the cell you point at, and on the cell you select. Click the number, or just start typing, to enter one. Only whole numbers of zero or more are accepted.
- **Add phase** — The toolbar button in the phase view creates a new project phase. You can optionally pick a phase template (see below) to pre-fill its batches.
- **Add batch** — The same button in the batch view creates a new batch within the selected phase.
- **Column menu** — Click a phase or batch name in the header row to rename it, **Set multiple numbers** for several designs at once, clone it or delete it. The batch menu also has **Prefixes** and **Hide batch** (a hidden batch is not shown in the viewer).
- **Bulk → Load numbers from project splitter** — Replaces the matrix with the counts stored by the IFC splitter.
- **Bulk → Reset numbers (to actual existing constructibles)** — Recalculates the matrix from the units that already exist. This also deletes the quantities saved on the project, so it asks for confirmation first.

Quantities are **saved automatically** a couple of seconds after you stop editing. The toolbar shows *Unsaved*, *Saving…* or *Saved*, with a Save button while there is anything pending, and it also saves when you leave the view.

### Saved is not the same as generated

*Saved* means your numbers are stored on the project. It does not mean the panels exist: the matrix is a plan, and the units are only created or deleted when you press **Generate**.

So the **Generate** button says whether the two agree:

- When they do not, it is filled and carries the difference — `Generate  +42 / −3`, units to create and units to delete. Hover it for the detail.
- When they do, it is drawn in a lighter style, because pressing it would change nothing.

There are two ways to make them agree:

- **Generate** — create and delete units so production follows the matrix.
- **Bulk → Reset numbers (to actual existing constructibles)** — discard the numbers and read them back from the units that exist.

The numbers on the button are what **Generate** would actually do, so a difference it reports is always a difference you can act on.

### Keyboard

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| Arrow keys | move between cells |
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> / <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>Tab</kbd> | next / previous column |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> / <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>Enter</kbd> | next / previous row |
| type a digit, or <kbd>F2</kbd> | overwrite the value |
| <kbd>+</kbd> / <kbd>−</kbd> | step the value by one |
| <kbd>Delete</kbd> | set to zero |
| <kbd>Esc</kbd> | cancel editing, or clear the selection |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>D</kbd> | copy the selected value down the column |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>V</kbd> | paste a column of numbers copied from Excel |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Z</kbd> | undo |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Y</kbd> or <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>Z</kbd> | redo |

A fill-down, a paste, *Set multiple numbers* or *Auto-allocate by prefix* all undo in a single step. The **?** button in the toolbar lists all of this.

### Reading the matrix

The second column shows **assigned / target** for each design, frozen next to the design name. It turns green when the two match and amber (or red, in the batch view) when they do not — that is the number to watch while filling the matrix. In the batch view the target of a row is its phase quantity.

Above the matrix, a status bar totals the project: target, assigned, area, and how many designs do not add up. Hover the **target** figure to see which IFC file each part of it came from.

### Where the target comes from

The target is the number of units the IFC splitter found for each design. It is worked out from the splitter's own counts, so it updates by itself every time you split a file.

Actions in the **Bulk** menu, under *Project totals*:

- **Clear the project totals** — empties the targets. The splitter counts themselves are kept, so this is reversible.
- **Recover totals** — rebuilds the targets from every piece of splitter information available. It shows each design, where its number comes from, and what would change, before writing anything. The matrix is not touched.
- **Set totals into the matrix** (phase view only) — writes each design's project total into the phase columns.

Under *Project matrix* are the actions that change your plan rather than the targets: **Load numbers from project splitter** and **Reset numbers (to actual existing constructibles)**.

If **Recover totals** finds nothing, this project has no splitter counts stored — split the IFC again to rebuild them.

#### Projects without targets

A project you never split has no targets, and neither does a design you added by hand. Those rows show only the number you assigned: no target, no colour, no balance button, and they are not counted as not adding up. The status bar drops the target figure too. Nothing to compare against, nothing claimed.

The same applies per design, so a project where only some designs came from a split judges those and leaves the rest alone.

### Balancing

- **Balance a row** — an unbalanced row has a button next to its assigned/target figure. It spreads the difference over the columns that already carry a number, keeping their proportions. If the row has nothing allocated yet, it all goes on the first column.
- **Balance all** — when rows do not add up, the status bar shows a red *N rows do not add up* button. It opens **Balance all** in the batch view and **Set totals into the matrix** in the phase view. Both are also in the **Bulk** menu, and both show which designs will change, and by how much, before you commit.

When a phase has many batches the matrix scrolls sideways. The design name and the target/assigned column stay frozen on the left, the header row stays on top, and the grand total stays pinned at the bottom.

## Phase templates and automation

These tools speed up setting up a phase and filling its batches. **Add panels for module counts** is in the **Bulk** menu of the phase view, and **Auto-allocate by prefix** in the **Bulk** menu of the batch view.

### Phase templates

A phase template is a reusable set of batches, defined once per company. Each batch in the template has a name and an optional list of **name prefixes** and a production line.

Templates are managed in **Projects Settings → Phase templates**, in an expandable section at the bottom of the page, and are available to all the projects of the company. When you create a phase, choosing a template automatically creates its batches in that phase, including their prefixes.

A phase created from a template shows a magic-wand icon next to its name. Open the phase menu and choose **Set phase template** to see which template is applied or to apply a different one — its batches are created or updated to match.

### Batch prefixes

Each batch can carry the name prefixes used for auto-numbering. A batch with prefixes shows a split icon next to its name. Open the batch menu and choose **Prefixes** to view or edit them. Templates fill these in automatically, but you can adjust them per batch at any time.

### Add panels for module counts

In the **phase view**, set how many of each module you want in a phase, then choose **Bulk → Add panels for module counts**. The panels each module contains are taken from the module's own parsed contents and set on the same phase, multiplied by the module count. This works whether you used the project splitter or only the module splitter.

A dialog asks whether to set the numbers in batches too:

- **Also batches** — set the phase totals and also distribute them into the phase's batches by prefix (so you can generate right away).
- **Only phases** — set just the phase totals and leave the batches untouched.
- **Close** — do nothing.

The panel totals are recalculated from the module counts each time, so clicking the button again does not double the counts.

Hover the tree icon next to a module's name to see its decomposition — the panel (assembly) design names and how many of each the module contains.

### Auto-allocate by prefix

In the **batch view** (with a phase selected), choose **Bulk → Auto-allocate by prefix** to send each design's phase number into the batch whose prefix matches the design name. When a name matches several prefixes, the longest (most specific) prefix wins. Designs that match no batch are reported and left unassigned.

Together these give a simple flow: place module numbers on a phase → add the panels for those modules → switch to the phase's batches and auto-allocate by prefix → generate.

## Generating Constructibles

Once your quantities are defined, click **Generate** to create the actual assembly and module instances based on the matrix counts.

The dialog works on one level at a time: choose **Modules** or **Assemblies** at the top. It shows how many units will be created and how many deleted, then the detail per phase and batch, before you commit.

![The Generate dialog](./generate-dialog.svg)

1. How many units will be created and deleted.
2. The detail per phase and batch. Deletions come first.
3. Quantities saved for designs or batches that no longer exist. They are discarded.

::: warning
For every design, the batch quantities of a phase must add up to that phase's quantity. If they do not, the dialog lists exactly which designs and phases are off and by how much, and generation is blocked until you fix them.
:::

Your saved quantities are only cleared once the units have actually been created. If generation fails, they are kept and you can retry.

Quantities are saved against the designs and batches you wrote them for. If any of those are deleted afterwards, their numbers can no longer be generated, and the dialog lists them as outdated quantities that will be discarded. Pressing **Generate** drops them and creates the rest.

## Area Metrics

The matrix shows areas in square meters next to the counts: the gross area of each design next to its name, the area per column in the assembly totals row, and the total assigned area in the status bar. This helps estimate material requirements and production workload.

pages.title: Issues Management
pages.body:
# Issues Management

The Issues view provides a centralized overview of all production issues and quality control records across a project. Open it from the project menu: **Production → Production Issues**.

[[toc]]

![Production Issues, with the detail of one issue open](./issues-view.svg)

1. The summary: all issues, and how many of each category.
2. The table. A tick in **Status** means the issue is solved.
3. **Edit issue**, **Solve issue** and **Delete**, in the detail panel.

## Overview

At the top, a summary card shows:

- Total issue count
- Breakdown by category: **Quality Control Issue** and **Production Issue**

Below the summary, a data table lists all issues of the project.

## Issue Categories

| Category | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| **Quality Control Issue** | Issues related to product quality, compliance, or inspection findings. They appear in the [Quality Control Report](/guide/reports/quality_control/). |
| **Production Issue** | Problems encountered during the manufacturing process (delays, equipment, material defects). They appear in the [Issues Report](/guide/reports/issues/). |

## Issue Fields

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| **Title** | Short description of the issue. Click it to open the issue detail. |
| **Text** | Detailed explanation of the problem. |
| **Category** | Quality control or production issue. |
| **Constructible** | The assembly or module affected, with its position in the batch. |
| **User** | The user who reported the issue. |
| **Created** | When the issue was reported. |
| **Status** | Open or solved. The table shows a check when the issue is solved. |
| **Pictures** | Optional photos or files attached to the issue. |

The issue detail also shows the design and its revision, and the engineering contact of the project when one is set.

## Creating Issues

Issues are created in the [3D Viewer](/guide/viewer/#issues): while viewing a constructible, click **Note** to report a problem directly from the production floor. You can attach the data of the selected parts and pictures for context.

## Editing and Deleting

Hover a row to see its actions: **Edit issue** (title, text and category), **Solve issue** and **Delete**. The same buttons are in the issue detail.

## Resolving Issues

To close an issue:

1. Click **Solve issue** on its row or in the issue detail.
2. Select the design **Revision** in which the issue was solved.
3. Add a **Comment** explaining how it was fixed.
4. Click **Submit**.

The issue is then marked as solved, and its detail shows the revision and the solving comment.

## Sorting

Click a column header to sort the table by title, constructible, category, user, creation date or status.

pages.title: Reports
pages.body:
# Reports

Reports let you generate documents from your project data — Bills of Materials, production spreadsheets, QR stickers, quality control PDFs, and more.

[[toc]]

## Creating a Report

1. Go to **Production files** (machine files and shop-floor documents) or **Management files** (quality, worktime and issue reports). Both exist inside a project and company-wide, under the Files section of the menu.
2. Click **New production file** or **New management file**.
3. In the report form dialog:
   - Select the **Report Type** (e.g., Plates BoM, Production Excel). The list only shows the types of the view you are in, and machine files only when one of your machines produces them.
   - Optionally add a **Document comment** and pick a **Document status** (*For information*, *For ordering* or *Temporary*). In PDF documents the status is printed in the page header and the comment on the cover page. The comment is also added to the file name.
   - Configure the **Document settings** specific to the report type.
   - Choose which **assemblies or modules** to include.
4. Click **Submit** to queue the report for generation.

![The report form](./report-form.svg)

1. The **Report Type**.
2. The **Document status**, printed in the header of PDF documents.
3. The **Document settings** of the type. **Form Content** shows them as JSON.
4. More choices for some types: here, the materials to include.
5. The assemblies or modules to include. Ready ones are marked, and so are multipanel groups.
6. **Submit**. The arrow next to it holds **Save without generating** (see the tip below).

::: tip
When you edit an existing report (pencil icon), the arrow next to **Submit** offers **Save without generating**. It stores the changed settings without creating a new version. **Submit** saves them and generates a new version. For a new report, both start generation.
:::

## File Defaults

Each document type has a set of options — cover page, how parts are grouped, table style, paper size, and so on. **File settings** lets you set what those options start at, per type, for the whole company.

Open **File settings** in the Files section of the company menu, expand **File defaults**, and pick a type. The types are listed under *Production documents* and *Management documents*. The form is the same one you see when creating the file. Save, and every new file of that type starts from your values.

- A type with nothing saved shows **System defaults** and uses the values built into Produuz.it.
- A type you have configured shows **Custom defaults**. **Reset** puts it back to the system values.
- Files already created keep the settings they were saved with. Changing a default never changes a document you generated earlier.
- Files generated from a template use these defaults too.

![File settings: File defaults](./file-defaults.svg)

1. A type with defaults of your own. **Reset** puts it back to the system values.
2. A type that uses the values built into produuz.it.

**Machine files are not in this list.** Their options depend on the machine model, so their defaults live on the machine setup, in **Production settings → Machine Settings**.

## Generation Templates

A generation template is a saved set of files you always create together — for example a Plates BoM, a Wood BoM and the QR stickers for the same panels. Instead of filling the report form three times, you pick the template, select the panels once, and every file in it is queued in one action.

Templates are managed in **File settings** → **File generation templates**, under the Files section of the company menu. Each file in a template is one document type, plus the machine or production line it should use when the type needs one.

To use one, open a project and click **Run template** in Production files or Management files, choose the template, select the panels and click **Generate**. You can also create a template on the spot with **New template** in that same dialog. Templates run inside a project only: in the company-wide views the dialog asks you to pick a project first.

## Report Status

![Production files](./reports-table.svg)

1. **Run template** and **New production file**. The field next to them filters the list by machine or production line.
2. The status of the last generation: a chip, or a bar while it is working.
3. A newer IFC arrived for some of the designs in this report. Hover it to see which.
4. The row actions: download, delete, edit, set as final, clone and generate again.
5. The versions of the report, under an expanded row.

Once submitted, a report goes through these stages:

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **initializing** | Queued for processing; the job will start shortly |
| **Working** | Being generated (a progress bar is shown) |
| **ready** | Successfully generated — use the download button |
| **failed** | An error occurred during generation |

When a report fails, you receive a message in the app if **Errors on report generation** is on in your notification settings. Whether that message is also emailed depends on your email settings.

### Document status

The **Document status** column is separate from the generation status. It says what the document is for: *For information*, *For ordering* or *Temporary*. The check icon in the row actions sets a report as *Final*.

## Versioning

Each time you regenerate a report, a new version is created: with the reload icon in the row, or by editing it and pressing **Submit**. All previous versions are kept. Expand the row to see the version history, where each version (rev 0, rev 1, …) can be downloaded or deleted. The download button in the row always gives the latest version.

::: info Design Updates
If a design's IFC file is updated after a report was generated, a red warning icon appears next to the report's status. Hover it to see which designs have a newer IFC. The same icon marks those panels in the report form. Regenerate the report to include the latest design changes; the warning then goes away.
:::

## Content Selection

Most reports require you to select which content to include:

- **Assemblies / Modules** — Select items from the project tree (phase → batch → panel). Panels that are already ready are greyed out and marked *ready*. **Sort by priority** orders the tree by production order. QR Stickers can include modules; the other reports work on assemblies.
- **Part Batches** — Some reports (Plates BoM, Wood BoM, Accessories BoM, the Wood and Plates CSVs and several machine files) have a **Select by Part Batches** switch to select part batches instead, which groups parts across assemblies.
- **Rack loads** — Rack Load Stickers are made for rack loads, picked from a list.

## Project Reports vs. Company Reports

**Project reports** are generated from a specific project's data. Inside a project, every report type is available, including all Bills of Materials, stickers and machine files.

**Company reports** are made in the company-wide Production files and Management files, when you need data across all projects. Only these types are offered there:
- Production Excel (Production files)
- Worktime Excel (Management files)
- Quality Control Report (Management files)
- Issues Report (Management files)

If your company plans production by date, the company-wide views offer the project types too. There you pick panels by **production line** and a **From** / **To** date range instead of a project tree.

## Report Types

### Bills of Materials

PDF documents listing the parts needed for your constructibles:

- [**Plates BoM**](/guide/reports/plates_bom/) — All plate parts with quantities and dimensions.
- [**Wood BoM**](/guide/reports/wood_bom/) — All wood/profile parts.
- [**Per-Design BoM**](/guide/reports/designs_bom/) — One BoM per unique design.
- [**Accessories BoM**](/guide/reports/accesories_bom/) — Accessories and hardware list.
- [**Custom Woods CSV**](/guide/reports/custom_woodcsv/) — Wood parts exported as CSV.
- [**Custom Plates CSV**](/guide/reports/custom_platecsv/) — Plate parts exported as CSV.
- [**Custom Accessories CSV**](/guide/reports/custom_accesorycsv/) — Accessories exported as CSV.

### Other Reports

- [**Production Excel**](/guide/reports/production_excel/) — Spreadsheet with one row per panel and its dimensions and areas.
- [**Worktime Excel**](/guide/reports/worktime_excel/) — Production time per panel, or per panel and station.
- [**Quality Control Report**](/guide/reports/quality_control/) — PDF summarizing quality control records.
- [**Issues Report**](/guide/reports/issues/) — PDF listing all issues found during production.
- [**QR Stickers**](/guide/reports/qr_stickers/) — Printable QR code labels for panels and modules, and Rack Load Stickers for rack loads.

### Machine Files

Machine-specific file formats for CNC equipment. See the [Machine Files](/guide/machine_files/formats/panel_mob1/) section for details.

pages.title: Plates BoM
pages.body:
# Plates BoM

The Plates Bill of Materials generates a PDF document listing all plate parts for your selected constructibles.

![A page of a Plates BoM](./plates-bom-page.svg)

1. The header of every page: project, status, date and batch, with your logo.
2. The material, finish and comment the table is for.
3. One row per plate, with zone subtotals and a total.
4. The plate drawings, numbered by the DWG Index of the table.

## Output

- **Format:** PDF (single file or ZIP with multiple PDFs)
- **Content:** All plate parts with dimensions, quantities, materials, and optional drawings. Plates are grouped by material, finish and comment. Each group has a *Clean Plates* table (plain rectangles) and a *Cutted Plates* table (plates with cuts or openings), with rows per zone, zone subtotals and a total of gross and net area.

## Options

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Group parts from the report in the same folder** | How the content is split into files (see below). Default: *By Batch*. |
| **Combine** | When the output is a ZIP, also add *Combined.pdf* with all the PDFs merged. |
| **Cover Page** | Include a title page with project information. On by default. |
| **Designs Summary** | Add a summary table listing all included designs. |
| **Totals Table Page** | Add a page with the gross and net area per material, before the tables. |
| **Show Plates Drawings** | Include plate drawings in the report. On by default. |
| **Attach to Viewer as DOC** | Link each generated PDF to its assemblies in the Viewer. Only when the output is a ZIP. |
| **Contact person** / **Delivery address** | Printed on the cover page. Leave empty to use the company's. |
| **Materials** | Only include plates of the selected materials. |

## Grouping Modes

- **By Selected Panels** — One single PDF with all selected content.
- **By Phase** — One PDF per phase (ZIP output).
- **By Batch** — One PDF per batch (ZIP output).
- **By Panel** — One PDF per assembly (ZIP output).

When you select by part batches, the output is always one single PDF.

pages.title: Wood BoM
pages.body:
# Wood BoM

The Wood Bill of Materials generates a PDF document listing all wood and profile parts for your selected constructibles.

![A page of a Wood BoM](./wood-bom-page.svg)

1. The material, section, finish and comment of the group, with a drawing of the cross-section.
2. The straight parts, with a totals row.
3. Parts that differ only in their length share one drawing. The part of the length that changes is drawn short, between two break marks.
4. The length reads **LENGTH**. Each end has its own 0.
5. One row per part, with its real length.

## Output

- **Format:** PDF (single file or ZIP with multiple PDFs)
- **Content:** All wood/profile parts with dimensions, quantities, materials, and optional drawings. Parts are grouped by material, section, finish and comment. Each group starts with a header (material, section code, finish, comment and a drawing of the cross-section), followed by a table per drawing with zone, reference, count, length, surface, volume, weight and counts per design, and a totals row.

## Options

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Group parts from the report in the same folder** | How the content is split into files (see below). Default: *By Batch*. |
| **cross section filter** | *all* (default), *shaped_cross_sections* or *rectangular_cross_sections*: include all parts, only parts with a shaped section, or only rectangular ones. |
| **Combine** | When the output is a ZIP, also add *Combined.pdf* with all the PDFs merged. |
| **Cover Page** | Include a title page with project information. On by default. |
| **Designs Summary** | Add a summary table listing all included designs. |
| **Totals Table Page** | Add a page with total length, surface, volume and weight per material, before the tables. |
| **Show Profile Side Drawings** | Include a side and top drawing for each part with details (drillings, notches, angled cuts), with its end-cut angles. On by default. |
| **Group parts that differ only in length** | On by default. Parts with the same details and a different length share one table and one drawing, with the length shown as LENGTH. See [below](#parts-that-differ-only-in-length). |
| **Attach to Viewer as DOC** | Link each generated PDF to its assemblies in the Viewer. Only when the output is a ZIP. |
| **Contact person** / **Delivery address** | Printed on the cover page. Leave empty to use the company's. |
| **Materials** | Only include wood parts of the selected materials. |

## Parts that differ only in length

With **Show profile side drawings** on, each wood part with a detail (a drilling, a notch, an angled end cut) gets a table and a drawing of its own. When several parts have exactly the same details and differ only in their length — the studs of a sloped wall, all with the same angled top cut — they now share **one table and one drawing**, with a row per part.

- The drawing shows the length as **LENGTH**, with no number. The real length of each part is in its row.
- The part of the length that changes is drawn short, between two break marks.
- Details before it are measured from the left end, below the drawing. Details after it are measured from the right end, above the drawing, each end with its own 0.
- Only the length may differ: a different width, height, section, material, finish or comment keeps the parts apart. Details must match within 1 mm.
- A part turned end for end or turned over counts as the same part. A mirrored part does not.
- A group has **one** changing length or none. If some parts change before a detail and others after it, they form separate groups.

Turn it off with **Group parts that differ only in length** to get one table per part again. The drawing of each part, in the viewer and in logistics, is not affected: it keeps all its numbers.

## Grouping Modes

- **By Selected Panels** — One single PDF with all selected content.
- **By Phase** — One PDF per phase (ZIP output).
- **By Batch** — One PDF per batch (ZIP output).
- **By Panel** — One PDF per assembly (ZIP output).

When you select by part batches, the output is always one single PDF.

pages.title: Per-Design BoM
pages.body:
# Per-Design BoM

The Per-Design Bill of Materials lists the parts per unique design. If multiple assemblies share the same design, the design is listed once, with the number of assemblies next to its name (for example `D-11 (x4)`).

![A page of a Per-Design BoM](./designs-bom-page.svg)

1. The design and how many of the selected assemblies share it.
2. One table per branch: timber, plates, and the branches you selected.

## Output

- **Format:** PDF, or a ZIP with one PDF per phase, batch or panel, depending on the grouping. Designs are deduplicated inside each file.
- **Content:** One section per design, starting on a new page: its wood table, its plates table, and a table for each selected branch.

## Options

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Group parts from the report in the same folder** | How the content is split into files: *By Phase*, *By Batch* (default), *By Panel* or *By Selected Panels* (one single PDF). |
| **table style** | *compact_tables* (default) gives one compact table per material type; *extended_tables* gives the full Wood BoM and Plates BoM tables, with drawings. |
| **Branches** | The custom branches to add as tables. Branches you do not select are left out. |
| **Combine** | When the output is a ZIP, also add *Combined.pdf* with all the PDFs merged. |
| **Cover Page** | Include a title page with project information. On by default. |
| **Designs Summary** | Add a summary table of all included designs. |
| **Show Profile Side Drawings** | Include the wood part drawings (extended tables). On by default. |
| **Group parts that differ only in length** | On by default. Parts with the same details and a different length share one table and one drawing, with the length shown as LENGTH. See [below](#parts-that-differ-only-in-length). |
| **Show Plates Drawings** | Include plate drawings (extended tables). On by default. |
| **Attach to Viewer as DOC** | Link each generated PDF to its assemblies in the Viewer. Only when the output is a ZIP. |
| **Contact person** / **Delivery address** | Printed on the cover page. Leave empty to use the company's. |

## Parts that differ only in length

With **Show profile side drawings** on, each wood part with a detail (a drilling, a notch, an angled end cut) gets a table and a drawing of its own. When several parts have exactly the same details and differ only in their length — the studs of a sloped wall, all with the same angled top cut — they now share **one table and one drawing**, with a row per part.

- The drawing shows the length as **LENGTH**, with no number. The real length of each part is in its row.
- The part of the length that changes is drawn short, between two break marks.
- Details before it are measured from the left end, below the drawing. Details after it are measured from the right end, above the drawing, each end with its own 0.
- Only the length may differ: a different width, height, section, material, finish or comment keeps the parts apart. Details must match within 1 mm.
- A part turned end for end or turned over counts as the same part. A mirrored part does not.
- A group has **one** changing length or none. If some parts change before a detail and others after it, they form separate groups.

Turn it off with **Group parts that differ only in length** to get one table per part again. The drawing of each part, in the viewer and in logistics, is not affected: it keeps all its numbers.

With *extended_tables*, custom branches set as *wood alike* get the same timber tables as the woods: straight parts in one table, parts with details with their drawing, grouped by length where they can be. With *compact_tables* they keep their compact table.

## When to Use

This report type is ideal when you want a complete BoM per design type rather than per physical assembly. Useful for purchasing and material planning where quantities are calculated per design variant.

pages.title: Custom Woods CSV
pages.body:
# Custom Woods CSV

The Custom Woods CSV exports wood and profile part data as CSV files, which can be opened in spreadsheet applications or imported into other systems.

## Output

- **Format:** ZIP containing one CSV file (or XLS file) per group
- **Content:** Wood/profile parts with the columns you select: Material, Wood Size W*H, Width, Height, Length, Part Count, Part Reference, Project, Panel Name, Finish, Comments and Shape Name. All are on by default.

## Options

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Export CSV file as XLS file** | Write each file as XLS instead of CSV. |
| **Add column names in the first row** | Add a header row. |
| **Remove Index column** | Leave out the index column. |
| **Separator** | `;` (default) or `,`. |
| **Decimal separator** | `.` (default) or `,`. |
