pages.title: Production Excel
pages.body:
# Production Excel

The Production Excel generates a spreadsheet with one row per panel of the project, with its dimensions, areas, weight and openings. It is listed in **Production files**.

![The Production Excel sheet](./production-excel.svg)

## Output

- **Format:** Excel (.xlsx)
- **Content:** One sheet. The first row holds the company name and the project name. Then one row per assembly with these columns:

| Column | Unit |
|--------|------|
| Phase, Batch, Order, Design | |
| Count | always 1 |
| Length, Height, Thickness | mm |
| Wall Area, Net Area, Opening Area | m² |
| Weight | kg |
| Opening 1 … Opening 4 | name of each opening |

A **TOTALS** row at the bottom adds up the count, the three areas and the weight. The header rows stay frozen while you scroll.

## Scope

Generate it inside a project: it always includes every assembly of the project, so there is no panel selection. Modules are not included.

::: warning
The company-wide Production files also offer the Production Excel, but there it has no way to pick panels yet and produces a sheet with headers only.
:::

## Options

There are no document settings. Only the **Document comment** and **Document status** of the report form apply.

## When to Use

Use this report for production planning meetings, or when you need the panel sizes and areas of a project in a spreadsheet.

pages.title: Worktime Excel
pages.body:
# Worktime Excel

The Worktime Excel generates a spreadsheet with the production time of each panel, taken from its checklist records. It is listed in **Management files**.

![The Worktime Excel sheet, one row per assembly and station](./worktime-excel.svg)

## Output

- **Format:** Excel (.xlsx)
- **Content:** One sheet. Cell A1 holds the company name and C1 the project name (*all* for a company-wide report). Row 3 holds the column names, then one row per assembly (or per assembly and station):

| Column | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| Assembly | Short panel ID (first 8 characters) |
| Phase, Batch, Order in batch | Where the panel sits in the project |
| Production Line | Line of the panel's batch |
| Production Station | Only in the per-station format |
| Design | Design name |
| Start datetime / Ready datetime | When the panel (or station) was started and finished, in the company's time zone. *Not started* / *Not ready* when there is no record. |
| Production time (mins) | Sum of the station times, from each station's start to its ready, counted in the company's working hours |
| Factory time (mins) | Working minutes from the panel's start to its ready |

Times are only filled in for panels that are ready; the others show 0. A **Total time** row at the bottom adds up both times.

## Scope

This report is available both at **project level** and **company level**.

- **Project level** — Includes every assembly of the project. The dates in the form are not used.
- **Company level** — Includes the assemblies whose scheduled production date falls between **From** and **To**. Set both dates: they start empty.

## Options

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Worktime Excel Format** | Choose how rows are organized (see below). Required. |
| **From** / **To** | Scheduled production date range (company-level reports). |

## Format Options

- **By constructible rows** — One row per assembly, with its total times.
- **By constructible-station rows** — One row per assembly and station of its production line, showing the start, ready and time of each station separately. An assembly whose batch has no production line gets a single row.

::: tip
The *By constructible-station rows* format gives more detail about where time is spent in the production process, which is useful for identifying bottlenecks.
:::

## When to Use

Use this report for labor tracking, cost analysis, and production efficiency reviews.

pages.title: Quality Control Report
pages.body:
# Quality Control Report

The Quality Control Report generates a PDF summarizing the quality control records of your assemblies.

![A page of the Quality Control Report](./quality-control-page.svg)

1. The checklist of each station, with who ticked each task and when, and the form values.
2. The pictures, each with who uploaded it.
3. The quality control issues of the assembly.

## Output

- **Format:** PDF
- **Content:** One section per assembly, with its production checklist (every task, per station, with its pictures and form values) followed by the quality control issues logged for it. An assembly with no checklist says so, and an assembly with no quality control issues says *no issue registered*.

## Scope

This report is available both at **project level** and **company level**. In both cases you select the assemblies to include.

- **Project level** — Select the assemblies from the project tree.
- **Company level** — If your company works by date, pick a production line and a date range to narrow the list, then select the assemblies.

## Options

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Table style** | How the checklist is printed: classic tables (the default), compact tables, or one table per station. |
| **Contact person** | Printed on the document. Leave it empty to use the company default. |
| **Delivery address** | Printed on the document. Leave it empty to use the company default. |
| **Production line** | Narrows the assemblies you can select (company-level reports). |
| **Date range** | Narrows the assemblies you can select (company-level reports). |

## Who did what

Every checklist item in the report says **who ticked it**, and every picture says
**who uploaded it and when**. The two are separate on purpose: the person who
takes the photo is often not the one who ticks the box.

The name is the **alias** of the employees who were working under the account at
that moment. When nobody was named — an older record, or an account with no
employees selected — the account name is shown instead. A picture uploaded before
this was recorded shows no name in the report, rather than borrowing the name of
whoever ticked the task.

The same information is on the panel itself, in the **Production Proof** card of
the constructible detail page, where such a picture says *No author recorded*.

See: [Who is working](/guide/viewer/#who-is-working) for how employees are
selected on the shop floor.

## When to Use

Use this report for quality audits, compliance reviews, and tracking quality trends across your production.

pages.title: Issues Report

pages.title: QR Stickers
pages.body:
# QR Stickers

The QR Stickers report generates printable QR code labels that can be attached to physical constructibles (assemblies and modules) for quick identification on the shop floor. It is listed under *Labels and Stickers* in the report type list of a project's **Production files**, next to **Rack Load Stickers** (see [below](#rack-load-stickers)).

## Output

- **Format:** PDF with **By Selected Panels**; a ZIP with one PDF per phase, batch or panel with the other **Make files** options.
- **Content:** One sticker per selected constructible, sorted by phase, batch and order in batch. Each QR code links to the constructible's Viewer page, and in the PDF the QR is also a clickable link. Each sticker prints the project name and number, phase, batch, order in batch, date, the design name (with its revision when it is not 0) and a short panel ID (the first 8 characters of the panel's unique identifier), so panels can be identified by eye without scanning. The banner formats also print the client name.

## Options

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Make files** | *By Batch* (default), *By Phase*, *By Panel* or *By Selected Panels*: how the stickers are split into files. |
| **Paper size** | Choose the sticker layout (see formats below). Default: *A4 - 4 QRs*. |
| **banner filename** | Which of your uploaded sticker banners to print. Used by the formats *with banner*. |
| **Client Meta** | Comma-separated property keys of your panels to print on each sticker, for example `montagevolgorde,level`. The value is taken from the panel, or from its design when the panel does not have it. A key found on neither is left out; an empty value prints `---`. |

## Paper Formats

| Format | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **A4 - 4 QRs** | A4 landscape, 4 large stickers per page (2 × 2). No banner. |
| **A4 - 4 QRs (with banner)** | A4 landscape, 4 stickers per page, each with the company banner on top. |
| **A4 - 12 QRs (with banner)** | A4 portrait, 12 smaller stickers per page (2 columns × 6 rows), each with the banner. |
| **Dymo (159*104) (with banner)** | One sticker per 159 mm × 104 mm label, for Dymo label printers, with the banner. |

![A4 - 4 QRs](./sticker-a4-4.svg)

1. The QR code. In the PDF it is also a link to the constructible.
2. The design name, with its revision, and your own client properties when you pick them in **Client Meta**.
3. The short panel ID.

![A4 - 12 QRs (with banner)](./sticker-a4-12.svg)

1. The banner, from the **Styles** card of the company page.

::: tip
The banner image is uploaded on the **Company** page, in the **Styles** card, under **Sticker Banner** (recommended size 1000 × 160 px). You can upload several banners and pick one per report with the **banner filename** option.
:::

## When to Use

Print QR stickers and attach them to assemblies or modules in the factory. Workers can scan the QR code with the produuz.it app or any QR reader to instantly open the Viewer for that constructible.

## Rack Load Stickers

**Rack Load Stickers** print one label per [rack load](/guide/logistics/delivery/), to fix on the rack itself. Create them in a project's **Production files**: pick *Rack Load Stickers* as the report type and select one or more loads in **Rack loads**.

- **Format:** PDF, one A4 landscape page per rack load.
- **Paper size:** *A4 - Single page* is the only format.
- **Left half:** a large QR code with *Scan to open this rack* under it. Scanning it opens the rack load on a phone or tablet; in the PDF it is also a clickable link.
- **Right half:** the load name, the rack name and type (*A-frame, both sides*, *Single side* or *Flat bed*), the number of panels and the load status; the **Delivery date** in large print when the load has one; the project, project number, client and location; the rack drawing; and the panels in loading order (first row fixed to the frame), with a dot on the strapped rows. The load's full ID is printed at the bottom.

![A rack load sticker](./sticker-rack-load.svg)

1. The QR code opens the rack load.
2. The delivery date, printed large.
3. The rack drawing, with the strapped rows in blue.
4. The loading order. A dot marks the strapped rows.

pages.title: MOB v1 Machine File
pages.body:
# MOB v1 Machine File

The MOB v1 is a text-based machine file format used to send manufacturing instructions to automated timber wall panel processing machines like the Mobi One.

![The report form for a MOB machine file](../panel_mob2/mob2-report-form.svg)

A MOB v1 file is created from the same form, with **MOB v1 Machine File** as the report type. The options of each station are in its **Station Job Options** block, and the file needs a production line.

[[toc]]

## What It Contains

A MOB v1 file describes all the operations needed to process a wall panel. It is organized into **layers** (representing different faces/sides of the panel), each containing a sequence of **operation commands**.

### Layers

Each layer represents a work zone on the panel:

- **Inside layers** — The inner face of the panel.
- **Center/wood layers** — The framing structure (studs, plates).
- **Outside layers** — The outer face of the panel.

### Operation Types

| Operation | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| **Framing** | Beam cuts, angle cuts, vertical and horizontal cuts for frame members. |
| **Nailing** | Line nailing patterns with configurable spacing for fastening cladding and battens. |
| **Plate positioning** | Cladding plate placement coordinates. |
| **Milling** | Routing paths, circles, and ellipses for openings and cutouts. |
| **Sawing** | Transverse cuts across the panel. |
| **Drilling** | Hole positions for connections and hardware. |
| **Gluing** | Adhesive application lines for bonding. |

## File Structure

The MOB file is plain text with semicolon-terminated command rows:

```
VERSION 3.00;
TXT # MOB Conversion by Produuz.it;
REIHE inside;
ELN DesignName;
ELM max_x, max_y, height, scale, 0, 0;
Layer [zone details];
[operation commands]
End Layer;
```

Each command has a code (e.g., `NRZ`, `BR`, `PSG`) followed by numeric parameters defining positions, dimensions, and tool settings.

## Generation Options

When generating MOB v1 files, the report form shows these options per station:

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Production starting side** | Machine zero mode (walls or floors), and a second field to begin processing from the inside or outside face. |
| **Shift mode** | How operations are shifted between layers: No shift, Shift on layers, Shift on operations. |
| **File generation with operations that exceeds the machine sizes** | Trim operations up to max size, Do not generate the layer, or Generate it anyway. |
| **Use Custom Matrix pattern** | Use the custom framing nail matrix of the machine setup. |
| **Plates nailing pattern** | Regular pattern, Large panel pattern, or Single Nailing Optimized (BETA). |
| **Mill and saw directions** | Clockwise or counter-clockwise for the inside and outside contours and holes. |
| **Tool assignments** | Which nailer, screwer, saw, mill, drill or glue unit to use, per zone and side. |

The CTC spacing of plate nail lines is set in the machine setup (**Default value for CTC in plates nailing**), not in the report form.

## Output

- **Format:** ZIP containing one `.mob` file per assembly
- **Requires:** A production line with a configured machine (Mobi One V1 or Frame Station V1)

## MOB v1 vs. MOB v2

| | MOB v1 | MOB v2 |
|---|--------|--------|
| **Machine** | Mobi One V1, Frame Station V1 | Mobi One V2, Frame Station V2, Robobrick, Isolation Machine |
| **Carriages** | Single carriage | Up to four tool carriages, read from the machine configuration file |
| **Flooring** | Not supported | Flooring stations, set in the machine setup |
| **Tool control** | Basic tool selection (one tool per type) | Several tools per type, including twin nailers |
| **Complexity** | Simpler, widely used | More advanced, newer installations |

pages.title: MOB v2 Machine File
pages.body:
# MOB v2 Machine File

The MOB v2 is an advanced panel assembly file format for the H&M Mobi One V2, Frame Station V2, Robobrick and Isolation machines. It extends MOB v1 with support for several tool carriages, flooring stations, and more granular tool control.

![The report form for a MOB v2 file](./mob2-report-form.svg)

1. **MOB v2 panel file** as the report type.
2. The document status.
3. One **Station Job Options** block per station with a machine, holding the options of this page.
4. The production line the file is made for.
5. The assemblies to include.
6. **Submit**.

[[toc]]

## Output

- **Format:** ZIP containing one `.mob2` file per panel, named `<panel>_rev<revision>.mob2` and sorted in folders by phase and batch
- **Target machines:** Mobi One V2, Frame Station V2, Robobrick, Isolation Machine
- **Requires:** A production line whose stations have one of these machines. The report form shows one **Station Job Options** block per station with a machine.

## Parameters

These are the options of a Mobi One V2 station. The labels are the ones shown in the report form.

### General

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| **Production starting side** (walls / floors) | Machine zero mode: 'walls' or 'floors'. This field and the next one carry the same label in the form. | walls |
| **Production starting side** (inside / outside) | Begin processing from the 'inside' or 'outside' face. | inside |
| **Shift mode** | How operations shift between layers: 'No shift', 'Shift on layers', 'Shift on operations'. | Shift on operations |
| **File generation with operations that exceeds the machine sizes** | Handling oversized operations: 'Trim operations up to max size', 'Do not generate the layer', or 'Generate it anyway'. | Generate it anyway |

### Framing

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| **Use Custom Matrix pattern** | Use the custom framing nail matrix of the machine setup instead of the automatic one. | Off |

### Cladding Options

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| **Plates nailing pattern** | 'Regular pattern', 'Large panel pattern', or 'Single Nailing Optimized (BETA)'. | Regular pattern |
| **Minimum panel height for twin nailing** | Panels shorter than this height (mm) always use single nailing, even when a twin nailer is configured. 0 disables the limit. | 0 |

### Mill Directions

Section **Milling Mill directions**.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| **Inside Contour** | Mill direction for the contour on the inside face. | Counter Clockwise |
| **Outside Contour** | Mill direction for the contour on the outside face. | Clockwise |
| **Inside Holes** | Mill direction for holes on the inside face. | Clockwise |
| **Outside Holes** | Mill direction for holes on the outside face. | Counter Clockwise |

### Saw Directions

Section **Sawing Saw directions**. The same four settings for sawing: **Inside Contour (Saw)**, **Outside Contour (Saw)**, **Inside Holes (Saw)** and **Outside Holes (Saw)**. When a saw direction is not set, the matching mill direction is used.

### Tool Assignments

Sections **Cladding Tool IDs** and **Processing Tool IDs**. Each field only offers the tools that the machine configuration file declares as present.

| Tool type | Fields | Tool IDs offered | Default ID |
|-----------|--------|------------------|-----------|
| **Cladding nailer** | Plates Nailer Tool ID zone 1–3 Inside / Outside | 24, 25, 26, 44, 45, 46, 24+44, 25+45, 26+46, Single nailing from model, Twin nailing from model | 5 |
| **Cladding screwer** | Screwdriver Tool ID zone 1–3 Inside / Outside | 0, 1 | 0 (disabled) |
| **Batten nailer** | Battens Tool ID zone Inside / Outside | 24, 25, 26, 44, 45, 46 | 25 |
| **Mill tool** | Milling tool id | 28, 48 | 28 |
| **Saw tool** | Sawing tool id | 23, 33, 43 | 23 |
| **Drill tool** | Drilling tool id | 22, 42 | 22 |
| **Glue tool** | Gluing tool id | 29, 49, 29+49 | 29 |

### Robobrick-Specific

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| **Use Opimized mode** | Use optimized brick placement sequencing. | On |
| **Max distance between Glue lines for joining them** | Maximum distance (mm) to join adjacent glue lines. | 100 |
| **UUID Export mode** | 'IFC GID (base64) (produuz.it standard)' or 'IFC GID converted to canonical UUID v4'. | IFC GID (base64) |

### Isolation-Specific

The Isolation Machine form has the two **Production starting side** fields, **Shift mode**, and:

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| **Export Isolation as CSV** | Also export the isolation data as a CSV file, added to the ZIP next to the `.mob2` file. | Off |

pages.title: BTL File
pages.body:
# BTL File (Wood Profiles)

The BTL format generates cutting instructions for wood profile processing machines. It's used by Hundegger and H&M Truss Master equipment for cutting studs, beams, and other timber members.

[[toc]]

## Output

- **Format:** ZIP containing `.btl` files
- **Target machines:** H&M Truss Master, Hundegger Speed-Cut, Hundegger Turbo-Drive

## Parameters

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| **Group parts from the report in the same folder** | How to organize output files: 'By Panel', 'By Batch', or 'By Phase'. | By Panel |
| **Split shared references per panel (By Batch / By Phase)** | Only when grouping By Batch or By Phase. Keeps a reference that appears in several panels as one entry **per panel** — each with its own quantity and its own panel fields — instead of merging them into a single line. Example: `P50` used 3× in one panel and 2× in another produces two entries (count 3 and count 2). | Off |
| **Split files by Profile Size** | Create separate files for each profile size. | Off |
| **Create Marks on parts** | Add marking operations on processed parts. | Off |
| **Include longitudinal cuts (bevels and rips along the part)** | Include cuts that run along the part. | On |
| **Number of decimals in angles** | Number of decimal places for angle values. | 1 |
| **Reference prefixes to filter** | Only include parts whose reference starts with one of the prefixes in the table. | — |

### Part data fields

The standard "Part data" fields that your machine/SCM software reads — **Designation, Assembly number, Group, Package, Material, Timber grade, Quality grade** and **Subgroup / Storey** — can be filled with whatever you want, per machine. They are in the **Part Data Fields** section of the form. Each field is a small template where you type free text and/or **properties** wrapped in curly braces (see below). This lets you export a whole **batch or phase** in a single file while every part still carries its own panel identity, instead of having to export panel by panel.

For example, setting **Designation** to `{part_pos} ; {assembly_name}` produces values like `5461 ; HD-529`.

The defaults are: Designation `{part_pos}`, Assembly number `{design_name}`, Material and Timber grade `{material}`, Quality grade `{description}`, and Group, Package and Subgroup / Storey empty. These fields apply to the BTL and BTLx files (not to the panel-frame BTL).

### User Attributes

You can define up to 5 custom attributes that are embedded in the BTL file. Each has a **name** and **value** field. Use these to pass additional metadata to your machine software.

### Properties

Both the part data fields and the user attribute values accept **properties** in curly braces, replaced per part — `{part_pos}`, `{assembly_name}`, `{material}`, `{batch}`, your own model properties, and so on. Each field has an **Insert property** button listing everything it accepts.

The full list, the rules and where else properties work: **[Properties in texts](/guide/properties/)**.

pages.title: BVX File (Hundegger)
pages.body:
# BVX File (Hundegger Wood Profiles)

The BVX format generates advanced wood profile cutting data for Hundegger machines. It offers more features than BTL, including material splitting, bench orientation, and void operations.

[[toc]]

## Output

- **Format:** ZIP containing `.bvx` files
- **Target machines:** Hundegger Speed-Cut, Hundegger Turbo-Drive

## Parameters

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| **Group parts from the report in the same folder** | How to organize output files: 'By Panel', 'By Batch', or 'By Phase'. | By Panel |
| **Split shared references per panel (By Batch / By Phase)** | Only when grouping By Batch or By Phase. Keeps a reference that appears in several panels as one entry per panel instead of merging them. | Off |
| **Split files options** | 'No split', 'Split by materials', or 'Split by materials and sizes'. | No split |
| **Part orientation** | Orientation of the part on the machine bench: 'Horizontal' or 'Vertical'. | Vertical |
| **Use voids** | Include void/cutout operations in the output. | Off |
| **Number of decimals in angles** | Number of decimal places for angle values. | 1 |
| **Reference prefixes to filter** | Only include parts whose reference starts with one of the prefixes in the table. | — |

### User Attributes

You can define up to 5 custom attributes embedded in the BVX file, each with a **name** and **value** field.

The value is a template: free text plus **properties** in curly braces, replaced per part — `{part_pos}`, `{assembly_name}`, `{material}`, your own model properties, and so on. The **Insert property** button on the field lists everything it accepts, and the full list is in **[Properties in texts](/guide/properties/)**.

Define milling passes at different depths in the **Milling steps by height** table:

| Column | Description |

| quantity | Number of identical parts |

| project | Project name |
| material | Material name |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|-----------|-------------|---------|

pages.title: Frame Nailer CSV
pages.body:
# Frame Nailer CSV

The Frame Nailer format generates nailing operation lists for H&M frame nailer machines.

[[toc]]

## Output

- **Format:** ZIP containing `.csv` files
- **Target machines:** H&M Frame Nailer

## File Contents

Each CSV contains nailing patterns and positions for frame assembly, mapping beams to nail positions based on beam dimensions.

## Parameters

### Framing Nailing Matrix

Define the nailing pattern based on beam size in the **Nailing Matrix by Beam Size** table (section **Framing Custom Sizes**):

| Column | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Beam Size** (mm) | Width of the beam. |
| **Top Padding** (mm) | Distance from the top edge to the first nail. |
| **Bottom Padding** (mm) | Distance from the bottom edge to the last nail. |
| **No of Nails** | How many nails per beam at this size. |

### Nailing matrix rows are size ranges

Off by default: each row applies to the exact beam size written in it, and a
size that is not in the matrix gets the automatic nailing.

Turn it on and every row becomes the **start of a size range** that runs up to
the next row, with the last row covering everything above it. A matrix with
rows at 89, 120 and 160 then nails 89-119 with the first row, 120-159 with the
second and 160 and up with the third, so you no longer need one row per
millimetre. Sizes below the first row stay outside the matrix.

pages.title: Mobi One
pages.body:
# Mobi One

The Mobi One (by H&M) is an automated timber wall panel processing machine. It handles the entire panel manufacturing process — framing, nailing, milling, sawing, drilling, and gluing — in a single station.

[[toc]]

## Overview

The Mobi One is set up as a **machine** linked to a **station** in your production line. When a constructible reaches that station, the system can generate MOB machine files with all the manufacturing instructions.

There are two versions:
- **Mobi One V1** — Single-carriage design, generates MOB v1 files.
- **Mobi One V2** — Dual-carriage design with expanded capabilities, generates MOB v2 files.

## Processing Units

The Mobi One can be equipped with various processing units depending on your configuration:

| Unit | Function |
|------|----------|
| **Framing** | Processes frame members (studs, top/bottom plates) |
| **Nailers** | High-speed pneumatic nailers for fastening cladding and battens |
| **Screwers** | Mechanical screw drivers |
| **Miller/Router** | Spindle for routing openings, cutouts, and milling operations |
| **Drill** | Multi-spindle or single-head drilling |
| **Saw** | Cross-cutting blade for transverse cuts |
| **Gluing** | Adhesive application system |

## Configuration in Produuz.it

### Machine Setup

In **Production Settings > Machine Settings**, create a setup with the model *H&M Mobi One V1 Station* or *H&M Mobi One V2 Station*, and link it to its station in **Production lines**. The **Machine setup** tab of the setup holds:

- **Layer orientation** — Inside, outside, or none.
- **X-axis mirroring** — Mirror operations along the X-axis if needed.
- **Machine zero position** — The reference point for the coordinate system: *File info* (the default, read from the machine configuration file), top right, top left, bottom right or bottom left.
- **Nailing matrix** — Customize nail patterns by beam size. The **Nailing Matrix by Beam Size** item in the Framing section opens its own window, which holds the matrix and the three settings below; **Apply** writes them back into the setup, which is saved with the setup's own **Save**. Each beam size row sets the top/bottom padding and the number of nails. The beam size is the height of the stud where it meets the rail. Rows are kept sorted by beam size when the setup is saved.
- **Nailing matrices by part class** — The matrix window can hold one whole matrix per **part class**: the matrix by beam size, the nail columns by beam width and their two range switches, all of them per class. Pick **Default** or a class at the top of the window; add a class with the field beside it, choosing one of the classes of your parsing setups or typing a new name. A stud whose class has a matrix is nailed by it; a size or width with no row in that matrix falls back to the default matrix, and then to the automatic nailing. This is how a panel that mixes I-beams and solid studs of the same height gets two nails on the I-beams and five on the studs. See: [IFC Parsing Setup](/guide/management/ifcps/)
- **Nail columns by beam width** — Next to the matrix, a second table decides how many **columns of nails** a stud gets from its width: set *No of Columns* to 2 or more and *Column Spacing* to the horizontal distance between columns, per beam width. The machine file then repeats the nail row at each extra column position. A width that is not in the table gets a single column. Its rows can also be read as width ranges with **Nail columns rows are width ranges**, exactly like the size ranges of the matrix, and they are kept sorted by width as well. The window that holds both tables shows a **preview**: type a beam height and width, and optionally a part class, and it draws the stud's joint with the nails the machine would drive, saying which matrix row or range answered, or that the automatic nailing applies, and warning when a column would fall outside the stud. The columns are drawn where the machine drives them: the first one 22 mm from the stud's edge (the nailer's offset from the X written in the file, which centres it on a 44 mm stud), the next ones one spacing further each.
- **Nailing matrix rows are size ranges** — Off by default, so each row applies to the exact beam size written in it. When on, every row is the start of a size range that runs up to the next row (the last row covers everything above it): rows at 89, 120 and 160 nail 89-119, 120-159 and 160 and up, instead of needing one row per millimetre. Sizes below the first row stay outside the matrix and get the automatic nailing.
![The nailing matrix window](./nailing-matrix.svg)

1. **Default** and one matrix per part class. Add a class with the field beside them.
2. The matrix by beam size: padding and number of nails.
3. Read the rows as size ranges.
4. The nail columns by beam width.
5. The preview: the joint as the machine nails it, and the row or range that answered.

- **Processing thresholds** — Minimum mill radius, CTC distances, and other tolerances.
- **Treat extra woods as normal frame woods** — Off by default. When off, extra woods (extra top/bottom wood and extra frame wood profiles) are handled as reinforcements: the extra rails are placed as ordinary horizontal pieces and get ledge nailing. When on, they are handled exactly like the rest of the frame: extra rails become top/bottom rails, they are nailed with the standard framing matrix, and they are included in flooring.

  This option is set **per station**, so each machine in the production line decides on its own. The typical use is a line where the frame station builds the frame without the extra pieces (option off) and a later station receives the panel with them already mounted (option on).

  A station with the option on also measures the panel from a different corner: because the extra pieces are already mounted, the panel is physically bigger, so its zero is the corner of the frame *including* them. Stations with the option off keep measuring from the structural frame, and an extra piece that sticks out lands on negative coordinates — the same as before.

- **Angular nailing** — Off by default. For machines equipped with a tilting nailer unit: nailer codes in the file are written with 4 digits (`00`, `10` or `20` in front of the tool number). Nailing along the panel contour, around windows and in the middle of a plate stays straight (`00` + tool). At a joint between two plates, the nail row on the left side of the joint gets `10` + tool and the one on the right side gets `20` + tool, so each row is driven at an angle into the shared wood. Every zone also gets a **Nail Context** drawing with the operation drawings, showing how each nail line was classified (contour, window, plate joint or plate face).
- **SVG Drawings** — All on by default. One switch per operation drawing generated with the machine files: Framing nails, Frame Glueing, Operations (plates nailing), Glueing, Bricks, Isolation, Battens, Batten Intersections, Plates Layout and the Nail Context debug drawing. Turn off the ones you don't use to skip generating them — the machine files themselves are not affected. In a production line with several stations, the switches of the machine that owns zone 0 (the frame) apply to the whole line.


### Job Settings

When generating machine files, configure per-job options, for example:

- **Starting side** — Which face to begin processing (inside or outside).
- **Shift mode** — How operations are shifted between layers.
- **Nailing pattern** — Regular, large panel, or optimized.
- **Mill direction** — Clockwise or counter-clockwise per zone.
- **Tool assignments** — Which physical unit to use for each zone.
- **CTC spacing** — Center-to-center distances for nail lines.

::: info
Job settings can be saved as defaults on the machine setup, in the tab of each file type it produces (for a Mobi One V2: *MOB v2 panel file*), so you don't have to configure them each time you generate files.
:::

## Generating Machine Files

1. Open **Production files** in the **Files** section of the left menu, in your project (or in company-wide mode, if your company works by dates).
2. Click **New production file** and pick **MOB v1 Machine File** (or **MOB v2 Machine File**) as the **Report Type**.
3. Choose the production line and select the assemblies to process.
4. Adjust job settings if needed.
5. Click **Submit** to generate.

The output is a ZIP file with the machine files (`.mob` for V1, `.mob2` for V2) and the operation drawings.

## Linking to Production

When the Mobi One station is configured in your production line, the machine files are available to production workers through the [Viewer](/guide/viewer/). The operations drawings button shows the machine processing sequence for each constructible.

pages.title: Frame Station
pages.body:
# Frame Station

The **Frame Station** is a machine type dedicated to the **frame layer** (zone 0) of a wall or floor panel — the structural frame of studs and top/bottom rails, before any cladding goes on.

[[toc]]

## Why a dedicated machine type

On most lines the frame is built on a Mobi One that also handles the cladding faces. Reusing that machine for the frame meant carrying a lot of settings that don't apply to the frame, and — more importantly — it forced the **inside** and **outside** faces of the frame to share a single configuration.

The Frame Station solves this:

- It only exposes the settings that are relevant to the frame layer (framing nails matrix, frame gluing, machine zero, etc.).
- It lets you configure the **inside** and **outside** faces **independently**, with a separate setting for each face where it matters.

It comes in two versions, matching Mobi One:

- **Frame Station V1** — produces **MOB v1** machine files.
- **Frame Station V2** — produces **MOB v2** machine files.

Both accept a machine configuration file upload, just like the Mobi One machines.

## Configuration in Produuz.it

In **Production Settings > Machine Settings**, create a setup with the model *H&M Frame Station V1 (MOB v1)* or *H&M Frame Station V2 (MOB v2)*. Then, in **Production Settings > Production lines**, link it to a station with **Machine station** and give that station zone **0**.

### Machine settings

- **General** — Machine zero, blocker heights, max wall length. (No generic direction switches here — orientation is set per face under **Face Inversion**.)
- **Framing** — Auto framing nail matrix paddings and minimum CtC, dynamic nail positioning, clamp deactivation. The **Nailing Matrix by Beam Size** opens in its own window from here: the matrix by beam size (height), with the option to read its rows as size ranges (each row covers from its own size up to the next one) instead of exact sizes, the table of **nail columns by beam width**, with its own ranges option, and one matrix per part class if you need them, with a preview of the nailing. Both tables are kept sorted when the setup is saved. See [Mobi One](/guide/machine_files/machines/mobi_one/#machine-setup) for how these tables work.
- **Face Inversion (per face, per axis):** whether each whole face of the frame is machined flipped. When enabled, **all** of that face's operations — woods, nailing, sawing, drilling, flooring and glue — are mirrored on the chosen axis. X and Y are independent and set per face:
  - **Invert X axis (outside face)** / **Invert Y axis (outside face)**
  - **Invert X axis (inside face)** / **Invert Y axis (inside face)**
- **SVG Drawings** — All on by default. One switch per operation drawing generated with the machine files, as on the Mobi One.

::: info
The inversion is applied to the whole face at once, so every operation of that face stays consistent with the others. It never affects the layer stacking (Z).
:::

## When to enable the face inversions

If the two faces of the frame are machined in opposite orientations and one face (typically the **outside**) comes out mirrored relative to the other, enable the X and/or Y inversion for that face. The whole face then follows the orientation the machine uses to machine it.

pages.title: Logistics
pages.body:
# Logistics

The Logistics view provides an overview of material requirements across your constructibles, helping you track which parts are available and which still need to be prepared.

[[toc]]

## Layout

The screen is laid out like the panel viewer:

- **The table**, with the branch and size pickers above it.
- **The toolbar**, a column beside it, holding the part batch, the search, the
  sorting, *Hide completed*, the columns, the button to mark all parts ready and
  every message the view has to give you.
- **The part panel**, showing the drawing and the properties of the part you
  picked in the table.

The top button in the toolbar, **Part data**, opens and closes the part panel:
with it closed the table takes the whole width. The choice is remembered on the device.

On a phone the toolbar becomes a bar at the bottom of the screen; press the
chevron and it opens upwards.

![The logistics viewer with a part batch running](./logistics-viewer.svg)

1. The panels of the project, ticked to put their parts in the table. With kit
   tracking on, each one shows how many of its parts are ready.
2. The branch and the size. The table shows one size at a time.
3. A zone header, with its own progress. See [Sorting](#sorting).
4. **Ready Parts**: type the number or use `−` and `+`.
5. The totals of the list.
6. **Part data** opens and closes the part panel.
7. The part batch block. See [Part Batches](#part-batches).
8. Search, sorting, *Hide completed* and the columns.
9. The drawings of the part you picked, and its 3D view.

## Material Tracking

The table shows one row per part to prepare, with these columns:

| Column | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Zone** | The structural area in the design where this part is used. Shown in the flat list only: when the table is grouped by zone, each zone is a header row instead. Projects without zones don't show it. |
| **Reference** | The part reference. Shaped parts (not a straight cut) carry an extra icon in front of it. |
| **Material** | Material name. |
| **Finish** / **Comment** | Only shown when some part in the list has one, because they split otherwise identical rows. |
| **Width** | Plates only. |
| **Length** | Length of the part. |
| **#** | Total number of this part needed across the selected constructibles. |
| **Counts by Constructible** | How many each assembly or module needs. The first two are shown as chips (grey: not started, orange: in production, green: ready), with the rest behind a `+N` chip. |
| **Ready Parts** | How many have been prepared. This column stays pinned to the right edge. |

Rows whose parts are all ready are tinted green. A totals line at the bottom sums
up rows, parts, ready parts, pending parts and the overall percentage.

## Sorting

Click a column header to sort by it. Each header you click is added to the sort
after the ones already active: click it again to reverse it, and a third time to
take it out. Zone and reference sort naturally, so `Z2` comes before `Z10` and reference
`9` before `114`.

The **Sort** menu has four ready-made orders:

- **Longest first** — the default, for cutting at the saw.
- **Reference A-Z** — to find a specific part.
- **Pending first** — to see what is still missing.
- **Zone then reference** — the kitting order.

The same menu switches between **Group by zone**, where each zone is a header row
with its own progress and the sorting applies inside it, and **Flat list**, where
the order applies to the whole table. Projects without zones always use the flat
list.

Your sorting, grouping, density and hidden columns are remembered on the device.

## Filtering

- **Branch** — One button per branch in the selection (for example `timber` or
  `plate`). If your production line is a logistics line, only the branches of
  that line are offered.
- **Size** — Filter to a specific material size. One at a time: this is a
  production view, and a run at the saw is one size. When the sizes do not fit
  in one row they move into a dropdown. The size cannot be changed while a part
  batch is running or paused.
- **Search** — Filter the table by reference, zone, material, finish or comment.
- **Hide completed** — Leave only the rows with parts still pending.

## Columns

The table only shows columns that say something different on each row. When
every part in the list is the same material — which is what usually happens,
since you pick a branch and a size before the list appears — the **Material**
column is dropped and the material is written once in the toolbar, as a chip.
The same goes for **Finish**, **Comment** and, on plates, **Width**.

The **Columns** menu turns **Material**, **Finish**, **Comment** and **Counts by
Constructible** on and off, and sets the row density: **Spacious**,
**Comfortable** or **Compact**. Spacious gives bigger `−` and `+` buttons for
touch screens.

## Selecting from a Report

Above the panel list in the left menu, **Select from report** takes the selection of a report and
loads it into the menu: pick one and the assemblies and modules it has selected
are ticked for you.

Only reports marked as **final** are listed — a document still being worked on is
not something to produce against — so the button is not there at all when the
project has no final report yet.

## Part Batches

A part batch is a run of work: the parts you are about to cut, from the moment
you start until you finish and put the leftover material back.

The **batch block** sits in the toolbar, just below **Part data**:

1. **Pick a batch** in the **Part Batch** selector, if somebody prepared one for
   you in the parts list. Picking it makes the table show that batch and nothing else.
2. **Start production** — with no batch picked, this creates one out of what is
   on the table (your selection, the branch and the size) and starts it.
   **Start batch** does the same for the batch you picked. Either way, who
   started it and when are recorded, and from then on the counters work.
   Before that, the counters are locked and **All ready** is not there.
   If those parts are already in a batch that has been started, that batch is
   opened and resumed instead of a second one being started over the same
   work — one press, whether it was left running or paused.
3. **While it runs**, the block shows the progress of the whole batch, when it
   started, who started it and the time worked. **Pause** stops the clock; the
   counters lock again until you press **Resume**.
4. **Finish batch** — or marking the last pending part — opens the form to
   declare the material. A batch can only be closed once every part in it is
   marked ready.

![The part batch block in its four states](./part-batch-states.svg)

1. Nothing picked: **Start production** makes a batch out of what is on the table.
2. A batch prepared in the parts list, not started yet: **Start batch**.
3. Running: progress, start time, who started it and the time worked.
4. Paused: the counters are locked until you press **Resume**.

Several batches can run at the same time, and you can switch between them
whenever you want. If you leave a running batch — by picking another one, by
changing the selection, or by navigating away — you are asked whether to pause
the one you are leaving, exactly like leaving a panel with an open checklist in
the viewer.

Nothing happens automatically overnight: a batch stays open until somebody
pauses or finishes it.

### Declaring the material

The closing form, **Declare materials**, has one section per size in the batch,
plus one for **Accessories and other materials**. Each section has two lists:

- **Taken from stock** — what you took for this batch.
- **Material returned to stock** — what you put back.

Press **Add line** to add a line. What a line asks for depends on the material:
a length and a number of pieces for timber, a width, a height and a number of
pieces for sheets, and a description and a number of pieces for anything else.
A **Notes** field sits at the bottom.

Press **Confirm and close batch** to save and close. **Nothing to declare** closes
the batch without any lines; it is a normal outcome and needs no explanation.
If some parts are still pending, the form says so and both buttons stay off.

The employees currently working are shown at the top of the form, and the
declaration is filed under them.

Produuz.it does not keep stock levels: this declaration is sent onwards, to the
system that does.

![The Declare materials form](./declare-materials.svg)

1. The employees the declaration is filed under.
2. One section per size in the batch.
3. What you took and what you put back, side by side.
4. **Nothing to declare** closes the batch with no lines.

### Where the batches live

**Part batches** lists them all: status, production line, project, progress,
start, finish, time worked and who ran them, with a search and filters by status
and production line. Clicking the name opens a panel on
the right with the batch in full — its parts, its work sessions and the material
declared — and the buttons to open it in the logistics view, pause or
resume it, finish it and reopen it.

The view is in two places: in the **company menu**, where it lists every batch of
the company, and in the **project menu**, where it lists only the batches of that
project and drops the project column. Switching between All projects and a
project keeps you on the list.

The **production line** is changed from that panel. It is the only field of a
batch you can edit there, and it is saved as soon as you pick it.

Batches can also be composed by hand from the **Parts list**, by
selecting parts and assigning them to a batch. That is the place to build a
batch that mixes several sizes: the logistics view always works on one size at
a time.

## Marking Parts Ready

You can update the "ready parts" count for each material to track preparation progress:

- Click on the number to type it, or use the `−` and `+` buttons.
- Use the **All ready** button in the batch block, just above *Finish batch*, to
  mark every part of the running batch as ready. It asks for confirmation first,
  and the dialog says that it marks the whole batch, including rows the search
  or *Hide completed* keeps out of view.

## Kitted Parts

A **kit** is everything a panel is built from. While its parts are still being cut,
the panel cannot be assembled, and the production list says so.

### What production sees

On the panel list in the viewer, each panel carries one label:

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **13 parts left** | still being cut. Grey while nothing has been cut yet, orange once cutting has started |
| **Kitted parts** | every part is ready (blue) — this panel can be built |
| *(station marks)* | work has started; the station marks carry the row from here |
| **Ready** | the panel is built (green) |

There is only ever one label. A panel with no parts recorded shows none, because
there is nothing to report about a kit that does not exist. If a panel is started
while parts are still missing, the count stays on the row in red.

![Kit labels on the viewer list, and the Kit column](./kit-labels.svg)

1. Nothing cut yet: grey.
2. Cutting has started: orange.
3. Every part is ready: **Kitted parts**.
4. Started with parts missing: the count turns red, followed by the station marks.
5. Built: **Ready**.
6. The **Kit** column of the Constructibles list. See [In the Constructibles list](#in-the-constructibles-list).

### Where the count comes from

A panel is kitted when **all of its parts are marked ready** in the logistics
table. Parts that were replaced by a newer revision do not count — they are no
longer part of the panel.

A **module** is kitted when every panel it contains has been **built**, and its own
loose parts are ready. A module cannot be assembled until its panels physically
exist, so a panel that merely has a complete kit is not enough.

### Choosing who decides

In **Company settings**, press **Settings**: under *Company Workflow Settings*,
the **Kitted parts** field has three options. Only company admins see the
button.

| Option | Who decides |
|---|---|
| **Off** | nobody. Nothing about kits is shown anywhere |
| **Manual** | the logistics operator marks a panel kitted by hand |
| **Automatic** *(recommended)* | the ready counts decide, on their own |

With **Manual** or **Automatic**, every panel in the logistics menu shows its kit
progress as a fraction, such as `12/25`.

On **Manual**, you also get three ways to mark a kit:

- when every part of a panel you have selected becomes ready, a message in the
  toolbar names those panels, with a **Mark kitted** button;
- a tick beside each panel in the logistics menu marks that one panel;
- with panels ticked in the menu, a **Mark kitted** button above the list marks
  all of them after a confirmation.

Use the last two when you know the kit is fine even though the counts disagree —
an offcut used, a part cut outside the flow.

Marking a kit by hand never changes a panel's production status.

### Starting a panel that is not ready

If you start a panel whose parts are not all cut, the viewer says so and tells you how many
are missing. **You can always carry on** with **Start anyway**, or press **Cancel**. It is a
warning, not a block. It appears once,
when the panel is started, and not again when you move to the next station.

### In the Constructibles list

When kit tracking is on, the Constructibles list has a **Kit** column
showing the same thing as a fraction — `12/25` (orange once cutting has started),
`✓ 25/25` (green), or `—` when the panel has no parts. It sorts, so you can put the
panels closest to ready at the top.

### On the dashboard

**Ready to build** shows everything still to be built, per production line, split into
what can be built now, what is partly cut, what has not been cut yet, and what has no parts
recorded at all. The big number on top is what your factory could start today.

It sits next to **Active backlog**, which answers a different question: that one says where
your panels are in production, this one says whether their material is there. A line with
forty panels waiting and five kits complete is short of material.

## Part Drawings

When a part is selected, the right panel shows its drawings — combined, front, top, left and section views — for quick reference on the workshop floor.

Only views that show real features (cutouts, holes, bevels, non-rectangular profiles) are produced. If a particular view would just be a plain rectangle, it's skipped — the dimensions in the table already convey that. A part with no features at all gets no drawings.

For wood parts that aren't straight prisms (parts with cutouts, bevels or mitres), an extra **3d** button appears in front of the drawing view buttons. Clicking it opens the isolated part in an interactive 3D viewer, so any feature that's hard to read on a 2D drawing can be inspected directly. The button only shows up when this 3D model is available.

## Connection to Other Features

- Material requirements are derived from the designs and their BoM data.
- The [Delivery & Racks](/guide/logistics/delivery/) feature uses the logistics data to plan how completed assemblies are loaded for transport.
- [Reports](/guide/reports/) can generate Bills of Materials for ordering the materials tracked here.

pages.title: Delivery & Racks
pages.body:
# Delivery & Racks

The Delivery view is where you decide how finished panels will travel: you arrange them on racks,
and that arrangement drives the order the factory produces them in.

[[toc]]

## Delivery dates

A rack load has a **delivery date**: when it is due on site. Fill it in and the Delivery screen
sorts by it, soonest first, and marks anything past its date and not yet delivered as **Late**.

Leave it empty while the load is only a plan. An undated rack sorts last and is never late.

## When to use it

Rack planning happens **before** production, not after:

1. You arrange the racks the way the panels need to ship and be built on site.
2. That arrangement sets the production order.
3. The factory produces the panels.
4. Workers mark each panel as loaded on its rack as it comes off the line.

So the panels you are arranging have not been made yet. That is normal, and the view shows their
real status without treating "waiting" as a problem.

## Two things with two names

- A **rack setup** is a kind of rack your factory owns — an A-frame, a wall rack, a flat bed. You
  own several identical ones of each; the app does not track which physical unit gets used.
- A **rack load** is one rack filled with panels for one project.

## Rack setups

Manage them from **Rack setups** in the company section of the menu (it is there when your
company has the delivery module). Press **New rack** to add one.

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| **Name** | What people call this kind of rack. |
| **Loading pattern** | **A-frame, both sides**, **Single side**, or **Flat bed**. |
| **Strapped rows** | Which rows are tied to the frame. See below. |
| **Usable length** | How long a row can be. Panels placed side by side have to fit in it. |
| **Stack depth per side** | How much thickness you can stack away from the frame. |
| **Max panel height** | The tallest panel the rack takes. |
| **Max overhang per end** | How far a row may stick out past each end of the rack. |

The list also shows how many loads use each setup.

The sizes are guides, not rules. The app warns when a load goes over them and lets you carry on.

![The rack setup form](./rack-setup-form.svg)

1. The loading pattern decides which rows exist.
2. The diagram follows your choices: the orange bar is the rack, the strapped rows are blue with a
   padlock.
3. **Strapped rows**. See [Strapped rows](#strapped-rows).
4. The sizes, in mm. See [Overhang](#overhang) for the last one.

When a rack goes out of service, **archive** it with the archive button on its row. It
disappears from the dropdowns and every load ever made with it keeps working. The **Archived**
button at the top shows archived setups again. Deleting is only possible for a setup no load has
ever used.

## Building a rack load

In the project menu, **Delivery** opens the planning view, with one card per rack load. Press
**New rack load**, or *Edit* in the menu of an existing card. The editor opens in three columns:
**Load details**, **Panels to load**, and the rack.

1. Pick the **Rack setup** on the left. The `+` button next to it creates a new setup on the spot.
2. Filter the panel list in the middle by production line, phase, batch or scheduled date. Those
   fields are a filter, not part of the load — they sit in their own boxed **Filter the panels**
   block, with a **Clear** button and the count of what is left underneath.
3. Click a panel to put it on the rack.
4. Drag panels to reorder them. Drag two into the same row to place them side by side. Drag onto
   the strip marked `+` to start a new row.
5. Fill in the description, the location, the **delivery date** and, if you use it, a status, in
   the first column. The status is free text.
6. Press **Save load**.

Rows tied to the frame are marked with a padlock. Which ones those are comes from the rack setup —
see **Strapped rows** below.

![The rack load editor](./rack-load-editor.svg)

1. The rack setup, with `+` to create one on the spot.
2. The filter of the panel list. It is not part of the load.
3. The panels that can still be added. Click one to put it on the rack.
4. A strapped row, marked with a padlock.
5. The capacity bar of a row. Orange here: the row hangs over the ends, within the allowance.
6. The orange question mark: this design has not been analysed, so its size is a placeholder.
   The vertical arrows on *W-14* mean it is taller than the rack takes.
7. Drop a panel here to start a new row.

### Reading the capacity bars

Each row has a bar showing how much of the rack length it uses, and each side shows how deep the
stack has got. Green is fine, orange is close (over 85 %) or hanging over within the allowance,
red is over. Nothing is blocked: you decide what fits.

A panel taller than the rack takes gets an orange vertical-arrows icon. If a panel on the rack
shows an orange question mark, its design has not been analysed yet, so the app is drawing it at
a placeholder size. Run the analysis to see the real one.

## Setting the production order

This is done where production order already lives: the **panel sorting dialog of a batch**.
There you get a **Sort by rack loading** button, which arranges the panels the way their racks
get loaded — load by load, and inside each one starting from the row against the frame. Each
panel also shows a small chip with its rack and its position on it, so you can check the order
against the plan before saving.

## The Delivery screen

Delivery is a mode of its own, next to Logistics and Production. Pick it in the mode buttons at
the top of the left menu and you get the racks instead of the panels: a row per rack load with how
far along it is, and the rack itself when you tap one.

The mode is there for managers, admins and production users when your company has the delivery
module.

It is built for a tablet standing next to the rack. Everything is a button you can see — there are
no menus to open and nothing hidden behind a long press.

### The list

Three tiles at the top filter it: **All**, **To load** and **To deliver** — the two jobs a rack
still has left on it. Each tile shows how many loads it holds. Tap one to filter, tap it again to
clear it.

Each row shows the load's description, delivery date, rack setup and location, and a bar with
where its panels are: green for delivered, blue for in the rack, orange for still to load. The state
(**EMPTY**, **TO LOAD**, **LOADING**, **LOADED** or **DELIVERED**) is written across the bar, with
your own status note in brackets after it and the count of loaded panels at the end. A rack past its
delivery date shows its date in red.

Pick **All projects** at the top and you get every rack the company owes anyone, soonest first,
grouped by project.

![The Delivery screen on a tablet, with a rack load open](./delivery-screen.svg)

1. **Delivery** in the mode buttons. With four modes, the productive ones share the right half:
   tap it to switch.
2. The filter tiles, with a count each.
3. A rack load: its bar, its state and how many panels are loaded.
4. A load past its delivery date shows the date in red.
5. The rack drawing. Tapping a panel points at its row in the list.
6. The three state buttons of each panel.
7. The buttons for the whole rack.

### Working a rack

Tap a rack to open it. You get the load's details and delivery status at the top, then the
drawing, the panel list and the buttons.

**Each panel has its own three buttons: Not loaded, In rack, Delivered.** One tap sets the state.
Nothing asks you to confirm: if you tap the wrong one, tap the right one.

Tapping a panel in the drawing points at its row in the list. The drawing is the map; the list is
where you work.

Along the bottom, three buttons for the whole rack: **Unload all**, **Mark all loaded** and
**All delivered**. Only *Unload all* asks first — the other two are undone by the button next to
them in one tap. Managers also get **Edit** at the top right, next to the refresh button, to change
the arrangement.

Printing the stickers stays in Reports, where it was: it is not something you do standing at a rack.

### Scanning

With a rack open, scanning a panel's QR marks that panel as in the rack instead of opening it —
which is what you want with the panel in your hands. If the panel is not on this load, the app says
so and changes nothing. Scan with no rack open, or scan any other code, and it works as always.

## Marking panels as loaded

Once panels come off the line, mark them:

- **On the whole rack** — *Mark all loaded* or *All delivered* from the Delivery screen, or
  *Mark all loaded* and *Mark delivered* on the load's card in the planning view. *Unload all*, on
  the Delivery screen, puts them all back.
- **One panel at a time** — the three buttons on its row in the Delivery screen, or the rack button
  in the [Viewer](/guide/viewer/).

This is what fills the delivery chart on the dashboard, so it is worth doing.

## Printing rack labels

Generate [Rack Load Stickers](/guide/reports/qr_stickers/) for a load. One rack per A4 sheet,
landscape. The QR takes the whole left half of the sheet, so it can be scanned from across the
workshop and at an angle. Beside it: the load name, the rack and its loading pattern, the
project, the project number, the client, the location, the drawing, and the panels in loading
order with the strapped rows marked.

The delivery date is printed large, above the project: it is what the driver looks for. A rack with
no date yet simply leaves it out.

Scanning the QR opens the rack on a phone or tablet, with the drawing, the panel list and the
buttons. Stickers printed before this change still work.

## Strapped rows

Some racks tie the first row down to the frame. Those panels are loaded first and come off last, and
the app marks them wherever they appear: with a blue padlock in the editor, in the Delivery screen
and in the drawing, and on the printed sticker with a blue row in the drawing and a dot in the
panel list.

Which rows are strapped is part of the **rack setup**, because it depends on the rack you own:

- **Flat bed** — nothing is strapped. There is no frame to tie anything to, so there is nothing to
  choose.
- **Single side** — **A0** (the first row) or **None**.
- **A-frame** — **A0**, **B0**, **A0 and B0**, or **None**.

The little diagram in the rack setup form shows it as you pick: the strapped row turns blue and gets
the padlock, and the rack itself is the orange bar labelled **RACK**.

Existing rack setups keep marking their first row, which is what they did before this was a choice —
except flat beds, which now correctly mark nothing.

## Overhang

Panels sit **centred** on the rack, so a row wider than the rack sticks out at both ends by the
same amount. How far it may stick out is part of the rack setup: **Max overhang per end**.

The bar under each row tells you where you are — green while the row fits on the rack, orange
once it hangs over but stays within the allowance, and red when it goes past it. It still lets
you save: as with the other rack dimensions, it warns and you decide.

A setup with the overhang left at 0 behaves exactly as before: anything wider than the rack is
over capacity.

## The rack drawing

The same drawing appears wherever the load does — the card, the rack's page, the rack button in
the viewer, and the printed sticker. One band per row in loading order, panels at their real
sizes, the strapped row highlighted, and the frame where it physically sits.

Each panel is drawn at its real width along the rack, with its name and its width × height ×
thickness written on it. On the printed sticker the panels are drawn as cross-sections, so their
thickness into the stack is to scale too. On screen each panel also shows its priority within its
batch as `number/total`, and a round badge once it is loaded (blue) or delivered (green).

Rows are centred and the frame is drawn at the rack's real length, so an overhang is visible
rather than implied; dashed guides mark where the rack ends.

It is drawn from the arrangement itself, so it is never out of date with what you saved.

![An A-frame rack drawing, with its capacity bars](./rack-drawing.svg)

1. A strapped row: tinted blue, with a padlock.
2. The frame, drawn at the rack's real length. Side B is above it, side A below.
3. The dashed guides mark where the rack ends.
4. This row is wider than the rack and sticks out at both ends.
5. The badge of a loaded (blue) or delivered (green) panel.
6. The capacity bars of the editor: red past the allowance, orange close to it or hanging over
   within it, green when it fits.

pages.title: Sizes and Materials
pages.body:
# Sizes and Materials

The **Sizes and Materials** view lets you manage your material catalog — the materials, sizes, and products used across your projects. Open it from **Sizes and Materials** in the company menu, under *Constructibles*. It used to be called *Stock products*.

[[toc]]

![The Sizes and Materials view, with Plate Size open](./sizes-materials.svg)

1. **New** adds an entry to the table that is open.
2. A plate size is a thickness of a material. The sheet dimensions you buy are products: see
   [Product Plate](#product-plate).

## Catalog Sections

The view contains five tables, each managing a different part of your material catalog. Each table starts folded: click its title to open it.

Materials and sizes are also created automatically when your designs are analysed, so most entries appear here without anyone typing them.

### Materials

The base materials used in production. Each material has a **Name**, a **Material Family** (wood, chipboard, gypsum or steel) and an optional **ERP Code**.

### Plate Size

The sheet materials by thickness. Each entry combines a material with a **Thickness**, plus an optional **Finish**, **Comment** and **ERP Code**. Reports and logistics use these to filter plates by size.

### Profile Size

The cross-sections of profile materials (structural elements like studs and beams). Each entry has a **Width** and **Height**, a material, an optional **Finish**, **Comment** and **ERP Code**, and an icon that tells rectangular sections from shaped ones. Whether a section is shaped comes from the design and cannot be changed here.

### Product Plate

The sheets you buy. Each entry has a **Name**, a plate size, and the **Width** and **Length** of the sheet.

### Product Profile

The bars you buy. Each entry has a **Name**, a profile size, and the **Length** of the bar.

## Managing Catalog Entries

For each table, you can:

- **Create** — Press **New** in the table's header to add an entry.
- **Edit** — Press the pencil on a row to change it.
- **Delete** — Press the bin on a row to remove it. You are asked to confirm.

::: warning
Deleting a material or size that is referenced by existing designs or reports may cause issues. Only remove entries that are no longer needed.
:::

## Connection to Other Features

- The material catalog feeds into [Logistics](/guide/logistics/) for tracking material availability.
- [Reports](/guide/reports/) use material and size data for Bills of Materials and filtering options.
- Machine file generation uses material properties to determine processing parameters.

pages.title: Integrations & Webhooks
pages.body:
# Integrations & Webhooks

Webhooks let an external system react to what happens in produuz.it. When an event you subscribed to occurs, produuz.it sends an HTTP `POST` to your URL with a JSON body you choose.

[[toc]]

## How webhooks work

1. You create a webhook in **Production Settings → Automations**, in the **Webhooks** card, picking the events it reacts to and the URL to call.
2. You pick which blocks of data go in the body (**Payload content**).
3. When one of those events happens, produuz.it builds the body and posts it to your URL.

**One webhook can hold several events.** If the same endpoint should hear about three of them, pick all three in the same webhook instead of creating three rows with the same URL, secret and headers. Every request carries `"event"`, so your endpoint always knows which one it is.

The number of webhooks you can have is limited by your licence, and the counter is shown in the card header (`3/10 Webhooks`). It counts rows, not events, so grouping events into one webhook uses less of your licence.

![The Webhooks card in Production Settings → Automations](./webhooks-table.svg)

1. The licence counter: green while you have room, red once you reach the limit, when **New** is disabled.
2. The production lines the webhook fires on. **All** means *Fire on every production line* is on. A warning icon means no line is selected, so the webhook never fires.
3. **Last delivery**: when the webhook last fired and how that call went. See [Delivery log](#delivery-log).
4. The row actions: **Deliveries** (the clock), edit and delete.

### What your endpoint receives

- Method `POST`, header `Content-Type: application/json`.
- The body always contains `"event"` with the event name, plus whatever payload blocks you enabled.
- produuz.it waits up to 5 seconds to connect and 10 seconds for your answer.
- **Any `2xx` counts as delivered** — `200`, `201` if you create a row, `202` if you queue the work, `204` if you answer with nothing. A `3xx`, `4xx` or `5xx` is recorded as a failure.
- **There is no retry.** If your endpoint is down, times out or errors, that notification is lost and nothing is re-sent. Every attempt is recorded, so you can see it happened — see [Delivery log](#delivery-log).

Calls are made by a background worker, not by the request that raised the event, so a slow endpoint of yours never slows down the tablet on the shop floor. Two consequences for your side:

- Expect the call **a few seconds after** the event, not at the same instant.
- **Order is not guaranteed.** Two events raised close together can arrive in either order. Use the `timestamp` in `serialized_event` if the sequence matters to you.

## Events

| Event | Triggered when |
|-------|----------------|
| `constructible_start` | An operator starts a panel or module in the production viewer (the panel checklist is opened and production begins). |
| `constructible_ready` | A panel or module completes its last station, or is marked ready in bulk from the constructibles list. |
| `station_start` | An operator starts one station for a panel or module. Also raised for each earlier station that is filled in when a panel is started at a later station. |
| `station_ready` | An operator marks one station as finished for a panel or module. Also raised for each earlier station filled in the same way. |
| `part_batch_start` | A part batch is started in the logistics viewer. |
| `part_batch_ready` | A part batch is finished in the logistics viewer. |
| `report_deprecation` | A new IFC is detected for a design and its existing reports are marked obsolete. |
| `rack_load_ready` | A whole rack load is marked *in rack* in one action. |
| `rack_load_delivered` | A whole rack load is marked *delivered* in one action. |

`unknown` and `mounted` rack statuses raise nothing: the first is an undo, the second happens on site. A rack load with no project raises nothing either.

The station events are the loudest of the list: one per station and per panel, so a line with six stations sends six times what `constructible_ready` sends. Starting a panel at a later station also fills in the earlier ones, and each of those raises its own pair. Subscribe to them when you track station occupancy; use `constructible_start` and `constructible_ready` when you only track panels.

## Configuring a webhook

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| **Name** | Free text, up to 80 characters. Only used to recognise the row in the table. |
| **events** | Which events trigger this webhook. Pick one or several. |
| **Fire on every production line** | Fires whatever the production line, including lines created later. Disables the list below. |
| **Production lines** | The production lines this webhook fires on. Select at least one: an empty list means the webhook never fires. |
| **Payload content** | Which blocks of data to include in the body. See [Payload content](#payload-content). |
| **auth header type** | `None`, `Secret` or `Bearer`. Adds an `Authorization` header. |
| **Secret / Token / SubscriptionKey** | The token sent after the auth header type. Only shown when a type is selected. |
| **URL** | The endpoint that receives the `POST`. Must be `http://` or `https://`. |
| **custom headers** | Extra HTTP headers, as name/value pairs. Press **ADD** for each one. |
| **custom payload** | Extra name/value pairs merged into the body. Press **ADD** for each one. |

The [NiceLabel tutorial](/tutorials/nicelabel/) shows the whole form filled in.

### Production lines

A webhook only fires on the production lines you select. Selecting none is not a shortcut for "all lines" — the webhook stays silent, and the form warns you about it.

If you want a webhook to fire everywhere, turn on **Fire on every production line**. That covers the lines you have today and any line you create later, so you do not have to come back and edit the webhook each time. With the switch off, a new production line is not added to your webhooks automatically: add it yourself to each webhook that should cover it.

Three events never belong to a production line: `report_deprecation`, `rack_load_ready` and `rack_load_delivered`. They reach every webhook subscribed to them, whatever lines it lists, and a webhook holding only those does not need a line at all — the form does not warn about it. An event on a batch with no line assigned is treated the same way.

## Payload content

**Payload content** is a multiple choice. Each option adds one block to the JSON body. If you save a new webhook without picking anything, it sends `serialized_event` only.

| Option | Adds |
|--------|------|
| `serialized_event` | The production event itself, merged at the top level of the body. |
| `serialized_station` | `production_station`: the station the event happened at. |
| `serialized_constructible` | `assembly` and/or `module`: the panel or module the event is about. |
| `serialized_part_batch` | `part_batch`: the batch, its session proof and the sizes it covers. |
| `serialized_project` | `project__details`: the project the event belongs to, with your own project number. |
| `employees__client_ids` | `employees__client_ids`: your own ids for the people the event belongs to. |
| `serialized_employees` | `employees__details`: the same people as full rows, with name and alias. |
| `nicelabel_print` | A NiceLabel print job, merged at the top level. See the [NiceLabel tutorial](/tutorials/nicelabel/). |

A block that cannot be built is simply left out — a station payload on an event with no station, for example. The request is still sent.

### `serialized_event`

The production event, merged at the top level. The account the event was posted from is deliberately not included.

```json
{
  "event": "station_ready",
  "uuid": "4b0a3f2e-6c1d-4a1f-9c2b-9f9b1f0f2a11",
  "timestamp": "2026-09-14T08:41:12.884Z",
  "project": "9d1e7b6a-2f44-4f0a-9a1c-1b2c3d4e5f60",
  "assembly": "e8f7e7f7-3b27-41e0-bb78-99eae64ba7cd",
  "module": null,
  "part_batch": null,
  "assembly_design": 45213,
  "module_design": null,
  "report": null,
  "employees": [312, 318],
  "employee_aliases": ["JAN", "PIET"],
  "meta": {
    "frontend_timestamp": "2026-09-14T08:41:12.640Z",
    "station_name": "Nailing",
    "station": "7a2c8e11-9d3b-4c22-8f1e-0b5a6d7c8e90"
  }
}
```

`employee_aliases` is a snapshot taken when the event was recorded, so renaming or removing someone later does not rewrite history. `employees` holds the matching account ids.

### `serialized_station`

Resolved from the station uuid in the event's `meta`, so it is only present on events that carry one: `station_start` and `station_ready`.

```json
{
  "production_station": {
    "name": "Nailing",
    "uuid": "7a2c8e11-9d3b-4c22-8f1e-0b5a6d7c8e90",
    "production_line_name": "Line 1",
    "production_line_uuid": "1c2d3e4f-5a6b-7c8d-9e0f-1a2b3c4d5e6f",
    "client_station_id": "ST-02"
  }
}
```

### `serialized_constructible`

Adds `assembly`, `module`, or both, depending on what the event points at. Both blocks have the same shape.

```json
{
  "assembly": {
    "uuid": "e8f7e7f7-3b27-41e0-bb78-99eae64ba7cd",
    "design_uuid": "db0cb2a6-8fbf-46ac-81f5-ece6faca584e",
    "design_name": "ML-0B-5",
    "status": "working",
    "scheduled_prod_date": "2026-09-15",
    "client_order_id": "1030622",
    "batch_uuid": "e8986e12-4454-4ae5-a40d-4929d6a5b789",
    "batch_name": "Batch 1",
    "phase": "Phase_1"
  }
}
```

### `serialized_part_batch`
